div.head: TRADR UNIONISTS AND TORYISM.
div.p: TRADR UNIONISTS AND TORYISM.

Sir,—lt was with interest I read in your issue of last Saturday the letter signed "Trade -Unionist,'-'-and could not but note the pointed remarks re the Trade Unionist Tariff Reform League, and think that one of the causes was in the organising of a dummy branch, with a leader whose trade union principles are nil. I fear that if the return of our worthy Mem- ber has to be left in the hands of the Trade Unionist Tariff Reform League its numbers will require a considerable move upwards, and its officers must be bona-fide trade unionists. A UNIONIST TRADE UNIONIST.

div.head: TEMPERANCE SUBURBS: A NOVEL SUGGESTION.
div.p: TEMPERANCE SUBURBS: A NOVEL SUGGESTION.

I Sir,—ln reply to " Aquam Bibo,". I would say that the tone of his letter is just splendid, and I hope to be able to reply in a like manner. Ile says that tremendous benefit would undoubtedly accrue to abstainers if temperance suburbs were adopted. I do wish that he had enumerated some of those benefits; but instead of that he begins with the difficulties. In answer to his first question: What chance of reformation, for instance, would remain for the inebriate? Well, as reformers, our work would not be quite so close at hand, that is true, but what is to hinder us from going to that work? And, having suc- ceeded in getting a man or woman to give up the drink, we could very materially help them to that end if we had temperance suburbs. Need I enlarge on this point? You know how many pledges are broken. The children would have all to gain, and the young people would have food for reflection when they saw such a marked difference in one part of the town from the other ' part. Question 2. Would I condemn a man who par- takes only of a nightly glass of liquor for, say, medical purposes, to pass the whole of his ex- , istenee in the community of drunkards, if he did not give up that glass? Well, I can only refer you to my first letter, in which it reads thus: "I am quite sure that the moderator would feel greatly obliged to us - - for clearMiL2ut, residentally, s)f course. anqwer to Mr- J. W. Bradley. - - - Well, he is in the fighting ranks, that is quite clear, but he-•?annot see- ter smoke. -Let us use the smokelesi' powder or 'temperance 'suburbs; then we shall see how the battle goe, and what - gains we are making on the enemies' forts. I will reverfTh My first letter, the main sub- stance of Which my two friends have either missed or ignored. I stated that I could never see. the wisdom or sense of justice in trying to get shorter hours, Sunday closing, reduction of licences, or in any way interfering with the trade. This, I believe, is a very smoky powder to use, as we cannot see what headway we are making, and it is also responsible for the "more strenuous opposition from the moderator." "J.W.8." has stumbled over a mistake in the composition of my first letter on this point, for which I humbly apologise. It is not our small numbers that troubles the moderator. Instead of it being a retreat to secure these temperance suburbs, it would be an advance in a straight and honest way, "something attempted, something done," and not like our present sneak- ing policy of local option with, total abolition to follow before it is due. Total abolition, I be- lieve, will not be due until we have brought all people over to our side. It will not be due even when we have gained a majority; that is only - the pdlitician'e way of thinking. Now the strenuous opposition to which I have referred before would cease if we took a more fair and reasonable stand. The moderator would then pee to it that his fellow workman, • the barman, should have his seventh day rest like he'has himself, and that is Sunday closing ,t at once. That they would make more safe- guards against drunkenness is my firm belief if they had no need to fear about risking the entire, loss of their present facilities. I think he will now begin to see what I mean when I refer to our, or, if he likes it better, his policy, as being I • both unwise and unjust. We do not go to live in a slum to abolish it,l and I have no doubt that both my critics now I . reside in the most decent neighbourhood that their means will
J. W. MEILOR.

div.head: INCREASING RENTS AND STANDARD
div.p: INCREASING RENTS AND STANDARD
WAtàrS,

Sir,—l have read with great interest the various letters on the above subject, especially Mr. Smith's admirable contributions. Owing to my occupation, I have had every opportunity to study tne remarkable difference that exists in the value of property in different parts of these isles. Whereas in Warrington, Manches- ter, Liverpool, &c., you have to pay from ss. 6d. upwardi; to get a good six-roomed house at weekly rental, in the Southern counties, such as Kent, Surrey, Wilts, &c., you can get the same class of house at least 35 per cent. cheaper. My friends, the trade unionists, will probably re- tort, "Yes, but the Southerner's wage isn't as much as the Northerner's." It is one of the greatest illusions that the hard-hearted North Country. xl4an has, that his financial position is immeasurably superior to that of- the Smith- erner. Such is not the case: The Southerner's wage (if a little lower) has a greater "pro' ratio" spending capacity. Then what is the real answer to "Why are rents increasing?" It can be solved (as Mr., Smith has already explained) in two words,l "Trade unionism." "Real" trade unionism would be the finest thing in the world for the industrial life of this country, both for the masters as well as the men. Probably about 90 per cent. of the present-day trade unionists are really good men. (each at his own particular trade), but the odd 10 per cent. are men who only join the union because they know that although their work is much inferior to that of their mates, their employer daren't dismiss them. If he did their mates, being union men, would, under threat of a strike, secure their re- instatement. As an example of the type of the odd 10 per cent., allow me to quote the following. As your readers are aware, at this time of the year there are several printers who advertise for " spare time agents" to get orders for Christmas cards. I have had several friends (who are well known for their staunch (?) trade unionism) approach me for an order. When I remarked "Why, I thought you were a trade unionist?" they have looked at me in surprise. It is just a "Spare pastime," they replied. Pas- time? I always thought that the sale of Christ- ians cards was part of a stationer's "trade." If that is their idea of trade unionism, then I am sorry for their cause. I think a good motto for them witald be "Do as we say, and not as

div.head: "" &DONAU'S PATENT SELF RAISING FLOM xFOSA74.OIIFEII THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1913
div.p: "" &DONAU'S PATENT SELF RAISING FLOM xFOSA74.OIIFEII THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1913

as we do." If they are trade unionists, why don't they go the whole hog? As Mr. Smith advises them, pay union prices for their tools, and make sure these are made by union work- men, &c.., , -It is absolutely impossible to have tr standard wage for every trade. Take my own particular trade. There are an enormous number of cheap cars on the roads now, which need little atten- tion or skill to keep them in running order. Is the driver of one of these entitled to the same' rate of pay as the man who has charge of famous and costly cars which, for workmanship and finish, are a triumph of the engineer and coach- builder's arts? What incentive would there be for a man to improve his knowledge and skill, if he knew that another man who is not near so skilled, is drawing the same rate of pay? None whatever.
By all means let us have a minimum "living" wAge. But to pay the " shoddy " tradesman the same wage as his more skilled mate is utterly unfair to the employer, and far more so to the men themselves.
FREE LANCE.
Thelwall, December 17, 1913

for building purposes, and deplored the fact that they omitted to use those powers, and he did refer to -the present Government's intentions to- wards an improvement in housing matters. But he should have gone further, and admitted that the Government have spied out the root of the evil, and surely any attempt to strike at this deserves more than a casual reference, made apparently• as an afterthought. It. does seem foolish to tax by excessive rating-improvements either in building or manufacturing, and it would appear that the way to find a remedy would be to alter the system, of rating and lease- holds. My advice, if a novice may presume to advise, is to watch Lloyd George._
Seeing that Mi.. Small has an objection to a "nom de plume," I sign my name with all due diffidence..
A. HORNBY RATIIBONE Latchford Without.

•Sir,—Mr. Smith has penned another column ' and a half to your valuable paper and is evi- dently indignant that anyone should question his own business, as a speculative builder, as a business beneath suspicion; and how amusing it is to find his comrades in the speculative building line up in arms, when one modestly ventures to suggest that any employer who apparently feels confident in his own righteous- ness should- at least set his own housO in order before publicly asserting •an undoubted trnth, viz., that .the wages of the Worker should he raised, in keeping with the increased cost oC living and limitless prosperity of the entwoying, class. I reiterate what I stated in my last letter? that 'had even the standard :Tate and fair condi- tions of labour been adopted by speculative builders in the erection of their property, your readers could, to some extent, understand the Afrontery of this section of the Property Owner's' Association spurring all owners to join their body, to make easy the increase of rents, whether wages went up or not. Mr. Smith, because of this, makes a spurious attack on the consistency and otherwise of trade unionists; and, with Out losing sight of the ques- tion, I joined issue with him on, I will pass opinion on the chief point's he raises. lie "wonders whether the house I live in was trade union,built; if so, do I pay additional rent on that account?" From inquiries made I think not; if it was, the woodwork is a dis- grace to my own craft. So far as rent goes, I have no control over the amount fixed, and if the rent goes up I shall have to pay up and look pleasant And this applies generally, " a trade union rent, whether trade union wages are paid or not."

M. Smith then sa•ys that "the whole tenor of my argument is that the property builder has gone to the wall because they did not em- ploy union labour." No such contention on my part, and here Mr. Smith complicates matters I stated in my last letter that "until the specu- lative builders recognised fair conditions" the sooner they give cottage building up the better. Personally, I do not regret to think that it would be•better if the mortgagee type of builder did go to the wall, and the .facilities conferred on municipal bodies made use of, and I believe that the Co-operative Societies are endeavouring to cope with the demand—more speed to them, for we shall at least know that they are erected under fair conditions. Your readers will see that if these bodies take the question up, no extra rent will be charged to pay interest to the mortgagee, which at the present time creates a curse, and the tenants are the victims. Mr. Smith then says that "the union did not support the speculative builder, though he paid the standard rate." I ask, can they be said to be paying the standard rate, when, on his own admission; they purchase ready-made joinery from unfair shops? It matters not to us whether the origin of this ready-made joinery be Canada, Norway, or Sweden; it takes no amount of genius to see that the Canadian door, which, working on Mr. Smith's own figures, costs 50 Per cent. less to buy than the English door, of the same size, "is made by sweated labour." When Mr. Smith's friend, Mr. Cooper, in deducting the price of the timber, 4s. 6d., from the price of the Canadian door, 4s. 9d., asks: Where does the labour come in? I somehow think he has been hypnotised ever since: This is one of the reasons why speculative builders' shops are blacked to our members. We claim that, at least, we shall not fix or handle _joinery, whether doors, windows, stairs, or any other join, requirement, made by un- fair conditions. '•

Mr. Smith says that "considering most of the timber used here is imported, and to meet ship- ding facilities it is cut to lengths and sizes," and whilst I agree that, to some extent, this is necessary, our mental vision would be indeed limited if we allowed our friend to gull us with the idea that timber was converted into doors, &c., before being imported here, to meet ship- ping facilities, or to lessen the cost of other timber, even though shavings and sawdust are not articles to import into this country. Mr. Smith says that "the union does not stand' for increased efficiency." I would say, with emphasis, that, so far as the building trade goes, speculative builders, without doubt, stand for "increased deficiency." The union, so far as I understand it, claims a level standard of wage to all its members, not in any way pro- hibiting the better craftsman from better pay. The union is endeavouring to establish a com- mon principle of humanity, "all for each and each for all." The union is endeavouring to destroy the selfish principle of the survival of che fittest, and to protect the weaker of our sect from tactics of the unscrupulous employer, who, admitting our cause to be right, are, in practice, diametrically opposed to us. Mr. Smith says the trade unionist, when pur- chasing his own personal needs, does not care whether the articles he buys were made by trade unionists, and, in consequence, thS builder would not agree to the terms of the union. I admit that, to a great extent, there is- indiffer.: once in the less progressive members of our unions, but it is untrue to say that the builder refused to comply with our terms because of this. From what I read of employere, they would, in the majority of cases, welcome the_day if the worker would forsake his union, -hi order that they may individually bargain e.itli him as to the conditions he should work under. With regard to the tools we purchase, u,e are, without doubt, charged a price for every tool we need fully in keeping with trade union con- ditions, and if the worker who makes them does not get a fair wage, it is no fault of ours. I will draw a parallel. The speculative builder erects a house on, cheap labour. A would-be purchaser .comes along, but on 'inquiring the Price of the house finds that if it may be his he Must pay the top= price. - Here we see the inconsistency of the unfair employer of labour; here we see how the purchaser and the worker are fleeced.

Mr; Smith says that the remedy for non-union labour is that we "should appoint inspectors to check; as far as possible, the goods bought and sold, and then in five years we should sichive a pure state of working conditions." I need not remind our-friend on this good advice that consequence, our members have been checked from fixing it.)y speculative builders, the Joiners' Society have already checked the manufacturedan j°i :el7 conseq used u d, as

Mr. Smith says that he "is not antagonistic to trade unionism." If we dare believe him to be serious, how is it we have no account Hoowf hiss inie ttnihbaetrshieliptakesasatha-anntaogpeeloltityhee disorganised worker by purchasing Canadian doors, ece.' and in So doing boasting that there is no wisdom in paying 7s. for a door when one can be bought for 45.? _

Perhaps a reflection on these points may enable the speculative builders to avert their steps, and prove that they who declare for higher wages for the industrial worker are in- tending to set the example. I am glad Mr. Cooper has joined in this ques- tion, and I really give him credit for his sin- cerity. He asserts that my charge (re the standard rate to joiners) is absurd. He "main- tains that he and his brother, Daniel Cooper, have always paid the standard rate," but Mr Cooper does not stop at this, for in order to safeguard his argument, he makes a noose, and after carefully placing it around his argument he unmindfully pulls the cord. And, alas! chokes it. And this is how he did so.. After maintaining that they paid the standard rate, he tells us that he buys the Canadian door, which costs 4s. 9d. each. Then he says that to buy the timber alone for' one of these doors costs 4s. 6d. He may well ask where does the labour come in? It needs no article on i'ree Trade or Tariff Reform to explain that they are made by sweated labour. Until Mr. Cooper and friends can prove that all joinery required by them is made and fixed -under fair conditions, their shops will centinue to be closed to our members. TRADE U EON tS

div.p: frittrs to the (Ettitor
continued.
INCREASING RENTS.

Sir,—' was wrong when I suggested that the innocence of Mr. Smith was assumed. It is not assumed. Before I proceed to the more import- ant matter contained in his reply, I notice he still insists that rents should go up, in spite of lower values. The same argument might be applied to houses built on Cuerdley Marsh; as a matter of fact they would cost more in con- struction, yet, can any of your readers believe they would. be of equal value, or obtain any- thing like the same rental to similar houses built in Gorsey-lane? This question of site values may be very galling to the landlord who does not possess them, but that is no reason why the tenapt of cottage property should be ex- ploited to make up differences. Meanwhile, Mr. Smith may console himself with the knowledge that sooner than later a greater proportion of the differences in site values will revert to the community which created them, and not to the owner, as at present. Site values will play an important part in the forthcoming rating re- form. Allow hie iiew to have it word or two in reply_ to Mr. Smith's very bold statement made last week, one that challenged contradiction and in- vited verification,, to the effect that, extra charges of £1 Bs. 6d. upon the rent cannot be met with- out a covering charge of no less than £3 us. 6d. and a rising of the rent to 6s. 4d. per week. Your readers would be struck with the prepos- terous unfairness of that statement, which, although not exactly true, contains within and behind it, the spirit which precisely I am up against, and the very thing which brings me into this correspondence. It does not matter for the moment who gets the difference of £2 35.; the important thing which does matter is why the tenant should be fleeced so unmer- cifully and so unblushingly.. Mr. Smith puts all the blame on the. rating authorities, as I ex- pected he would, and in a paragraph entirely taken up with this particular point, tries his best to explain it, but fails most miserably. I suppose he will put it down to my simplicity when I declare I can neither follow his argu- ment nor square it with any known rule of rating. I have even gone so far as to offer small prizes .among my acquaintances for a solution. but without success, and I confess it reads more like an extract out of a Tariff Reform leaflet than anything else I can think of. Anyhow. I think I can find a way out of the difficulty. which has less of the crow and goose method about it. The problem is how to recover a charge of £1 Bs. 6d. at the least possible loss to the tenant, starting from a gross rental of £l3, with rent ss. weekly, and assessment £7 10s., paying £2 9s. rates, and leaving it net rental of £lO These are Mr. Smith's figures, of course, and I need hardly say there is a very serious flaw in them to start with. Well off as we are in Warrington in this respect, there is no such thing as a £7 10s. assessment on £l3 gross rental, but if there was, the abatement of 30 per cent. would reduce the rates due to £1 195., instead of £2 98 , which leaves a net rental of £ll is., so that the landlord is the gainer to the extent of £1 on yh e which resti Mr. Smith's figures for rates and net renta wonderl. I wonder whether this was a trap intended for the unwary? In any case, landlord comes best off, according to my showing. t now me allgiv ti e parties eoens ernecaonnedonedly.wTa shouldsatisfy is raised to ss. Bd. per week, giving a gross rental of £l4 14s. Bd., rateable value £9, on which £4 2s. 9d. is due in rates, leaving a net rental of £lO 11s. 11d. Your readers can now make their choice between a weekly .reqt of ss. 8d or Mr. Smith's weekly rent of 6s. 4d., an,' if my solution of the problem- holds the field, it will he readily admitted that there is justifica- tion for my "nom de plume." 17th December, 1913.
FAIR RENT.

Sir,—l must confess to being somewhat of a novice at this problem of rents, but it has at- tractions even for those who do not at the moment come under the category of tenant. Hence my reason for joining in the discussion. Let me say at once that I know little of. the methods adopted-lin the assefting of proptrty, or the basis on which the assessments are made. But I am trying to learn, and perhaps have de- rived some knowledge, which I did' not possess before, from the correspondence you have already published. But I find the task I have undertaken, voluntarily, I admit, of following the mathematical calculations of your corre- spondents, is becoming somewhat complicated and bewildering, and I therefore seek further enlightenment. Mr. Smith, in his letter to you last week, weaves hi argument zround several items of rent and rates, beginning with £l3, the gross yearly rental of a six-roomed cottage ten years, ago. In this is included ..e2 95., which the landlord had to pay on behalf of the tenant for rates, leaving a *het rental of £lO us., which, presum- ably, was an economic rent at that time. An- other item is that of £1 Bs. 6d., in which is in- cluded 5 per cent. on £lB charged for improve- ments, and las. 6d. to meet increased rates. Now ,to the uninitiated, it would appear that it should be simply a matter of addition and divi- sion. That is to say, add .21 Bs. 6d. to £l3, and after making whatever provision may be neces- sary for increased assessment due to the higher rent charged to meet the enhanced outgoings, divide by 52- to arrive at • the fair weekly rent, but this omits that mysterious £2 35., which, he says, has to be handed over to the Borough Treasurer, being the differenee between £1 Bs. Gd. and £3 us. Gd., which he says must be charged to obtain the former amount, and also that other mysterious item of £4 12s:, which he says is actually what the Corporation charges for rates. I should like to. know more about these two items of £2 3s. and £4 12s. Perhaps Mr. Smith will oblige. • Then I should like to take Mr. Smith to task about that £lB for improvements. In his first epistle to the unrighteous he made it perfectly clear that the Corporation allows this to be paid back in seven yearly instalments, making us. 6d. per year. And yet he suggests that it is fair to charge the tenant at the rate of 5 per cent. on the fall £lB from the beginning, as though the landlord had paid the whole of the £lB. in one amount. I suggest that justice would be better met if an amount was charged which would cover 5 per cent. on £2 its. 6d. the first year, .£5 3s: the second yeai., and so on until £lB is paid. And I notice that Mr. Smith does not meet the charge that the extra rent put on to meet this ,cost of improvements becomes a permanent asset in the value of the property; and that therefore it is a fair proposition that the tenant should be charged with only half the amount. If it is so unimportant that it should not be knocked off, why put. it on? And how delightfully naive were Mr. Smith's concluding remarks in his letter in your issue. 111 November 29th. How delightfully simple his remedy to banish the troubles of the property ovg,ners ! And what charitable beings these builders have been! They, he says in effect, have been actuated by nothing but a public- spirited desire to see the labourers and artisans of ,Warrington suitably housed, and reproaches the manufacturers because they have been so sadly lacking in a similar virtue. Nay, indeed! he goes further, and says to the tenants: "Seeing that your iron masters, leather manufacturers, and soap makers have not also become builders, you must demand that they shall subsidise the builders out of the profits they cannot help making, since it is not by enterprise they make profits, but by simply running their works night and day, and thus dodging the rate collector." And this running night and day trebles the out- put. Does it? Where and how? If Mr. Smith can show, I Would suggest he is at his wrong job, and plenty of manufacturers will be will- ing to pay him handsomely for his services, and so relieve him of anxiety in regard- to his pro- perty. I have some sympathy for the demand for a fair wage, not, however, to subsidise the builder, but rather to subsidise the human body.

This is not to say that the builder is not en- titled to a fair return on whatever his outlay may be, but Mr. Smith has not, yet made it clear what that return should be. He seems, mQreover, to overlook the real sources of trouble, or at any rate to be very gentle with them. Ire admits of his own knowledge that, £70,000 worth Of property has been " grabbed " during the last three years. Did the manufacturers grab it? And if not, why not ask those who did to -take their share in footing the bill? In strict fairness • I -Must, of Course, admit that Mr. Smith did casually refer to the powers Possessed by CorpOritfOlS to advance moneys

div.head: TkIREATENED SUNDAY MORNING OAK Si:HUGE.
div.p: THE TkIREATENED SUNDAY MORNING OAK Si:HUGE.

Sir,—ln your issue of Saturday last you an-' uounce tut the Tramways \donnuittee have decided to discontinue the car service on Sun- day mornings. Tins is very much to 6e re- gretted, and 1, along with a great many others, sincerely nope that our w9rtily Aldermen and k:oulicillors who are members or this important committee will see their way clear to re-consider the question. If not, it will be a very serious matter indeed for the maty of the Noncon• formist churches and chapels in the town; not only will this mean empty places in the if wen- tag, but a large number will gradually aiift away and cease attending altogether. It will be another excuse for the indifference and laxity of which we hear so much at the present time.
It is all very well for the Rector and others similarly situated, having their flocks around their churches, to advocate this policy.

We aIL admire the motive of the -committee in taking thiesi course, viz., to giire the men a Sun- day off alternately. But, sir, -.1 respectfully sub- mit that this can be easily accomplished, with- out causing so much inconvenience to the general public. Why not reduce the service by one-half P Instead of a ten minute service, let us have one every twenty minutes. I have not yet seen a car, either on a Sunday morning or afternoon, but it could easily carry twice as many passengers. In the afternoon particu- larly, I have noticed that there are very few people using the cars, and yet in the afternoon, I understand, it is proposed to put on the telt minute service.

If this twenty minute service idea were adopted, just half the men would be required; consequently they could have their altdrnate Sundays off duty. I am sure that no one would mind getting up ten minutes earlier where necessary, to catch a car. Again, from the finan- cial point, of view, it would be far better, because, if the twenty minute service were adopted, the total receipts would probably be about the same as they are at present, and this at half the present expense. But if there be no cars the income will, of course, be entirely lost. W. T. WILLIAMS.
Sankey-street, 16th December, 1913.

div.head: NATIONAL SERVICE AND CONSCIENCE.
div.p: NATIONAL SERVICE AND CONSCIENCE.

Sir,—When I raised the question of the posi- tion of the conscientious objector under the Defence Acts of Australasia, I expected Mr. Townroe would say something about it in his reply. Merely to quote the clauses in these Acts is not .sufficient. I am quite cognisant of the wording of these so-called exemption clauses, but I wanted attention to be directed to the fact that these guarantees were proving ineffec- tive under the administration of these Acts. On the Nain point at issue Mr. Townroe appar- ently prefers to remain silent, and for obvious reasons. - _

• As far as the few figures are concerned which he has had the courilge to quote, he is correct. But let us proceed much further. He says "78 Territorials have been committed to detention in New Zealand." /t is well to remember- that most of these were boys. But these figures were only up to April 30th, 1913, and applied only to New Zealand. Might I add that even up to this date in New Zealand there had been 3,434 prosecutions. Had such a law been in force in Great Britain, the proportion for our population would have been over 3,500 gaoled and nearly 155,000 prosecuted! But what about Australia, which Mr. Townroe leaves severely alone? The authorities admit that 12,373 prosecutions have taken place up to May 31st, 1913. Nearly 300 lads 'have been imprisoned in military for- tresses! Comparing these latter figures on the basis of our own population, we get 3,000 lads gaoled and 123,730 prosecuted. lam giving these figures to indicate the dimensions of w-tat Mr. Townroe is pleased to call "a noisy but small band" of resisters.

Again, prosecutions in Australia under the Education Acts for truancy from school cannot be reasonably compared with Defence Act prose- cutions, for the whole position is quite different, and the comparison is totally unfair and mis- leading for the following reasons : (1) The excessive shortage of labour causes parents to keep their children from school to help on the farm, 8"

oy The number of school hours per year amounts to above 1,200, while the drill hours are 90 for senior cadets and 120 for junior cadets. On the basis of hours, vompulsory military training is at least eight times as unpopular as universal education.

(3) The prosecutions under the Education Act apply to girls as well as boys; the number of defaulting girls, therefore, needs to be deducted. (4) Under the Defence Act the boys have been prosecuted;. whereas under the Education Act the partnts are prosecuted. I trust Mr. Town- roe will have the courage to face facts. With regard to Lord Roberts's Manchester speech, I hope to write later. • The person _from whom-I received the information is out of town. I hope to corroborate my statements later. In the meantime I would advise Mr. Tovinroe to save his turkey from the general slaughter that is imminent, as it may be wanted later.. Allow me to extend my thanks to him for the generous offer, and heartily to reciprocate his greetings of good-will.
Jr. 'GRAY.

div.head: DISESTABLISHMENT AND DISENDOW-
div.p: DISESTABLISHMENT AND DISENDOW-
MEWL

Sir,—l was very pleased to sea Mr. Stidston- Broadbent's letter in your last week's issue, anti 4111 sorry that he has been mis-led on some 01 the chief points in my speech on Welsh Dis- astablisnment, which is accounted for, .1 believe, *ay his only, having the . summarised version before him. If lie had been at the meeting and heard the spoech his desire to rush into print might not have been so acute. To take his points singly will require valuable, space, but I do so, hoping that indulgence will be shown, considering the keen interest taken in this question locally.

The first charge, that I call myself a High Churchman, I confirm, and would refer Mr. Broadbent to the history of the Oxford move- ment, which since its inception, has consistently advocated Disestablishment. Much interesting information in support of this statement may be found in the speeches of Lord Halifax. Just exactly what is meant by "siding up" I do not know, but imagine it to mean that I am sup- porting my Nonconformist friends in their demand for Welsh Disestablishment, and even- tually for Disestablishment in England. What the attitude of my political assoeiates in hypo- thetical circumstances would be I cannot say, nor del consider it necessary to speid valuable time on vague speculations. Respecting the statement that my first remark was that the "Welsh Established Church was not in any way the National Church, but merely a branch of the Church of England in Wales." There is no confusion of fact here, neither un- true statement, but if Mr. Stidston-.Broadbent had been present he would have recognised that this statement referred to the Church of 'Eng- land in Wales at the present day, which, as 1 then stated, is simply a branch of the Church of England, consisting of four dioceses—St. Asaph, Bangor, Llandaff, St. David's—and can- not, therefore, especially when the fact is National Church, in any sense, be called the borne in mind that it only represents 25 per cent. of the Welsh people. . If Mr. Stidston- Broadbent's idea of a National Church is one representing 25 per cent. of the nation to whom it professes to administer, then I must disagree completely and entirely with him. But in a later paragraph Mr. Broadbent agrees with me that the Church of England in ‘Wales is really a branch of the Church of England and part of the Province of Canterbury, which justifies my statement that it is an alien Church. There is therefore no necessity for Mr. Stidston-Broad- bent to be nervous about my reputation. If Mr. Broadbent will search a little further back in the 'history of Wales he will find that long before the coming of Augustine the ancient Irish Church had established herself in Wales, and that Augustine merely converted parts of Kent. .The spread of the new teaching, however, gradually forced the Irish Church followers to the extreme -West. There is evidence that the Diocese of Bangor was established in 550 A.D., which was forty-seven years before Augustine landed, and it is also plain historical fact that the Christian community founded by Augustine was not organised and consolidated until the •7th century, the work betng carried out by Theodore of Tarsus. With the assumption (it is nothing else) that the Church of England at the present time is directly connected with the ancient Church of the Angles, I do not agree, and my critic must know that this is a highly con- troversial subject, and that the-orders of the Church of England are not recognised as valid by the Roman Catholic Church, in spite of the repeated attemptis to obtain the Pope's authority. If the present Established Church is assured of continuity from the Church of the Angles, why, then, petition the Pope for a declaration? And why does the present Church not revert to the practices of the ancient Church—High Mass, prayers for thedead, reser- vation of the Sacrament, &c., all of which were part of the, ritual of the Church of the Angles? The foregoing deals with, paragraphs 6 and 7; and with regard to my statement that many people believe the religion of the Church of England to be sinful, I can only refer Mr. Stidston-Broadbent to the many sects of Non- conformists in Wales and in this country who follow strictly the religion of their predecessors, also .to the members of the Roman Catholic Church. These people consider the service of the Church of England cannot possibly save a person, and they are entitled to their own reli- gious beliefs and opinions, hut it is not right or j ust that believing this they should be forced to, contribute by tithe, &e., to the upkeep and maintenance of creeds which they believe quite sincerely to be wicked. The sarcastic assumption that I do not know , the meaning of "Establishment" is exactly what 1 should expect from the majority of Lymm Tories, and I pass it with contempt-. Wisendowment is to me simply the recovery of property to which the Church of. England has lost all title, as, for instance, moneys left by pious people to pay for Masses for the repose of their souls, and which can he found better uses of value and (t o endowdec iar e dh sh thelccf hphiuruieleisaceidhin. towfDidttoal for than to pay a country vicar his salary for ministering to some 100-200 people, seeing that it is illegal for him to say Masses. Can this money be honestly taken by -the Church of • England? Again, how was the Church of Eng- land endowed after the Reformation? When Henry VIII. quarrelled with the Pope by reason of the latter refusing to sanction his immoral purpose, this saintly monarch decided, to estab- lish a Church for himself. His methods were particularly effective, and, in passing, I might say somewhat similar tO what is being carried out in Ulster at the moment—slow roasting over boilercathedrals, h e d rfiarless,, monasteries,4lo.fditisniieriree revenues,every- thing he Church on Earth. Some of these properties but I do not think they are Liberals, but man awh reeelrde. given.by t h memberse bi 13: es Mr. BroaAlbent agree with me Mat these lands and revenues should return to their lawful owners? Answering his query whether I am prepared ;to sacrifice considerably more than half ()Piny estate in pertain eventualities, I say: “-yes, decidedly, if the whole; or part of that estate had been obtained by me by the methods which were used to endow very largelys the pre- sent Established Church, or any part was received by me in payment of services which my conscience would not allow me to t er•ori " Edv eas tnh' aepti brssa' at usthi Henryp r churches,t e seizedrs and lands, are Will Mr. Broadbent say the same with respect to the Church of England's den owments? I doubt it!

My reasons' for. working for Disestablishment in Wales and in England were fully stated in my address, but I will briefly outline them for Mr. Broadbent's information: That an Estab- lished Church, controlled by a civil Govern- ment, is not competent to specify what ought tq be a- nation's creed, and cannot be supposed to have Divine ,authority; - that the maintenance of any particular system of religion under the patronage of a Government is anti-scriptural, unjust, and a violation of the rights of con- science; that the system of patronage is anti- quated and allows abuses, in so far as a patron can appoint to a living without consulting in the slightest the wishes of a congregation. The patron may be a Jew, a Roman Catholic, an Agnostic, or a total unbeliever, the only qualifi- cation required being that he has purchased the adrowson. This system tends to make ministers independent of the wishes of their flock, lazy and indolent, and leaves very little room for burnin% zeal and intense vitality. Under the present system no revision of the Prayer-book is possible, except by cumbersome and vexatious methods, taking years to complete. It is- -iny intense conviction that if the Church of Eng- land could throw aside her pretensions to exclu- sive treatment and concentrate her efforts and energies on the spiritual uplifting of the masses she would in a few years be easily the strongest and most powerful Church in the Country, but so long as she persists in maintaining an exclusive and arrogant position she can never hope really and effectively to carry out her Master's work. The average man cannot understand why in a Christian Church arch- bishops should receive <215,000 per annum, while poor curates burning with intense devotion, loving our Church, sacrificing their health, and very often. the health of their families, are com- pelled to drag out an existence on sometimes less than 30s. weekly. Under Disestablishment. with the right to manage our own affairs, and with the laity allowed more control than at present I believe these abuses and anomalies would be swept away. My appeal Was to all who had the cause of true religion at heart, to work with the small band of Liberal Church- men for these objects.
REGINALD BARKER.
Oak Lea, Statham. December 15th, 1913.

ENGLISH DEMOCiiAGY,
Its Rise and Growth Discussed at the Sankey Adult School.

div.head: FEATURES AT THE THER St,HoOLS.
div.p: FEATURES AT THE THER St,HoOLS.

At the Adult School, Sankes- Bridges, on Sun- day, Mr. Thomas E. Knowles gave a lecturette on "The History of English Democracy." Mr. Knowles traced in broad outline the stages by which government, at one time royal and per- sonal, had become in theory the instrument of the people. The Church, which in past cen- turies had struggled for sovereignty, failed because it was too exclusive; whereas the State had embraced an ever-increasing body of dis- sent. The -State, however, was not at first .a popular institution. Men were familiar with its exploitation by kings and privileged circles. In time, the idea prevailed that the less govern, meat there was, the less harm would be done to the people. The theory of laissez-faire developed under-government being favoured rath.3r than the risk of over-government. Naturally, the propertied classes preferred this policy. They, -however, mistook privilege for "liberty." Even men so humane as Bright and Cobden long resisted such mea:sures as the Factory Acts on the ground that they would ar- bitrarily interfere with the natural liberty of man to drive bargains with his tellcrws. . but those who possessed little preferred strong gov- ernment if they could control it. Government gradually became the affair of the people by the operation of the Reform Acts, ex- tending from 1632 to 1885. But it was realised that votes were of little use to men who did not know their value, and the passing of the Educa- tion Acts of 1870 and 1889 were necessary inci- dents in the development of democracy. Representative government, however, was threatened in certain garters, its operations failing to satisfy impatient and .revolutionary spirits. The strike afforded an example.

div.head: ACADEMY-STREET MEN'S.
div.p: ACADEMY-STREET MEN'S.

The Adult School is not content to rest on its laurels, but endeavours to forge ahead. Educa- tion is the desideratum, and a Literature Com- mittee has beei formed iro furnish cheap yet reliable booklets by well-known authors and specialists, dealing with the topics of the day. Last Sunday morning the President of the War- rington Sub-Union, Mr. John A. Ransome, paid a literature missionary visit to Academy-street, and submitted the bookstall scheme to the con- sideration of the members, with the result that it was decided to adopt it. Mr. Ransom° gave a racy and lucid synopsis of a number of the book- lets he had brought with him, dealing with "The Exposure of the War Trusts," "Adult School Aims and Methods," "Roman Fortifica- tions at Wilderspool," "Heroes of England," "Nationalisation of Railways," "The Great Illusion," "Labour Unrest: Cause and Cure," and a number of others on varibuitopics, all to be had for a nimble penny. The selection of the books is given careful- attention, books of general interest' being chosen; and those which speak of life and, its many complex present-day problems are finding a ready sale. The book- stall idea has caught on in all the Warrington Schools, and is hound to result in an increased and mere intelligent interest in questions of citizenship and general historic movements and literature.

div.head: DEWSEY MEN'S.
div.p: DEWSEY MEN'S.

On Sunday morning last a paper was read, -which had been written by a prominent leader of the Adult School movement. The writer dealt with the aims of the movement; he stated that for many people through the movement religion had become a living thing, something which is causing them to look out on life with a new vision of its possibilities, which had given them new standards of value. The message of Jesus had gripped their hearts and minds. Given a progressive expression amongst men of the spirit of Jesus, human society inevitably will be transformed as it .adapts itself to the new spiritual environments, and so a new social order will arise. The Adult Schools aie out on a very big business. Something has been formed which is vital, something which touches life at every point, something which is not of the nature Of a luxury, but absolutely essential to our well-being, something which determines the way in which the details of daily life are garded. In brief, that "religion is a growth out of the entire nature of man." Human life is rooted in the life of God, and must, if it is to fulfil God's purpose, reflect the character of God in the character and lives of men and women. Human history must be the story of a fuller. manifestation of the life of God in the life of humanity. If this be ohr conception of religion, it is to take part .in a social transformation and social revolution. Indeed, the Adult School movement is bent on raising the lives of men in all their applications and activities.

div.head: LONGFORD.
div.p: LONGFORD.

Mr. Elam on Sunday morning took the National Council Bible lesson, ." Paul's world- wide outlook," as his Subject. He described Paul as a "carpetbagger" amongst the band of early apostles of the Christian faith. Ire was a "globe trotter," going from city to citS, in Greece and Italy, planting churches and new societies wherever he went. Paul himself must have marvelled, as he remembered those ola days, when he was the strictest of the Jews and exclusiye in his religion- as a high caste Brahmin. To Paul everything was Christ to live, to work, even to eat and drink. Love to Christ had swept through his innermost being like a tornado. Like John Wesley in later times, Paul looked upon the wide world as his parish.

Comp Mots to Clever Vocalists.

Extremely well-rendered selections from the' were , given Mt the Legh,street „Primitive Methodist Church- On Sunday - after- iioon and evening by the choir of the church, -assisted by friends. In -the afternoon _the service was opened by .an overture on the organ, 'well played by Mr. T. H. Banner, followed by Mr. Levi Richardson, who gave a very sympathetic nndering of Comfort ye" and "Every valley." Mr. E. H. Pearce rendered, in his usual capable style, Thus saith the Lord" and "But who may abide," also " For behold" and "The people that walked in, darkness." Mrs. E. A. Sanders sang most tastefully," Be- hold a virgin" and "0 Thou that tellest." Mrs. C. Worthington Sang "There were shep- herds" with much taste, as also did Mrs. A. E. Hoyle in "Rejoice greatly." Other solos were rendered by members of the choir fir a very -creditable manner. The choruses "And the :glory," "For unto us a -child is born," "Glory to God," and "His yoke is easy,' were sung with expression and vigour. The Rev. A. 'J. The soloists were Mrs. E. A. Sanders, Mrs. C. -Worthington, Miss M. Jones, and Messrs. W. J. _Booth and B. H. Pearce. Mrs. Sanders gave a beautiful rendering of "He was despised," as ,ltid also Mrs. Worthington in "I know that my Redeemer liveth." Mr. Booth was heard to advantage in "But Thou didst•not leave," and Mr. Pearce was especially good in his interpre- tation of "Why do the nations?"

The choir deserve much praise for the man- lier in which they sung the choruses. The Hallelujah Chorus" was, as usual, a favourite, hut the choir excelled themselves ik their ren- dering of "Tie trusted. in -God." div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
BACON PRICES. The Chance of the British Farmer.
In an article in-,' The Times "_ on bacon prices and the question of prices, a correspondent writes :

The high-class -bacon has opine mainly from the big milk-producing countries. No One has discovered a food which will produce Such good quality pork as milk and barley meal, or good quality pork at a cheaper cost. Countries like Denmark, with a limited and poor agriculture, had to find new methods or starve. Their Governments sent out able men to search, and they saw that milk and pork would save them. They learned modern methods, established , dairy factories and bacon factories; taught their people, and encouraged them to support the factories. The cream was •converted into butter, and the skim or separated milk into pork; in which way they have proved suc- cessful. But tha ingenuity of- the scientist has shown that animal fats, less digestible than butter fat and far cheaper, cOuld be rendered into palatable margarine if worked up with milk. In fact, an attractive butter substitute, with the appearance and flavour of butter, could be obtained. Moreover, even the'ordinary analyst cannot definitely show to what extent animal fats kire used; Somerset house itself allows a considerable .perefttage of margarine in butter, because it had to be - admitted that up to a certain extent adulteration could not be detected. Every year butter-faking be- comes a more skilled art, and now. the quantity of milk, skimmed and whole, used in margarine making is enormous; moreover, it fetches more money for this than it will for pork-raising, with the result that less is being used for feed- ing pigs.

It is at this point where .the British pig-raiser comes to his own again. British farmers with a good fresh milk demand are not foolish enough to make butter in competition with the so-called butter, liut really milk-faked margar- ine, when to do so entails a loss of some pence a gallon as compared with that which it realises when sold to be consumed as new milk. With foreign milk being diverted from pig-raising, the British farmer is not invidiously placed; .the foreign raiser comes back to his mark. The opportunity ought not to be missed by British raiser. But factories develop slowl3ll, and the business must be regained by the in- dividual; further, the quality of the, bacon must be uniform, and to suit the palates of _those .who pay the highest prices. The older type of home-cured bacon went out of favour, and imiot likely to come into favour, excellent as undoubtedly much of it is whilst no hams equal many home-cured ones. Bacon .of thc

same type and quality as is produced in fac- tories must be made, It could be made, and uniformity might be secured if all were in- structed on similar lines. The outfit to allow a farmer .to produce light-cured bacon costs little. Individual farmers, or a collection of them, may work a village bacon-curing busi- ness, but to command a market for home-cured stuff it must be of one brand.
It is obviously the duty of county-counqs ,o provide the instruction and advice.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
Plant early gladioli in a light, rich soil if pos- ible. Mix plenty of grit with heavy soils. .Plant St. Brigid anemones fof April and May Lowering.

The mild weather has enabled garden work to be proceeded with until a much later gate than usual. Most plants are better divided up in the autumn and rooted cuttings and seedlings have a better chance of becoming established in an autumn like the present. Carnations should be put in their flowering quarters in the autumn. The roots should not be disturbed in the spring, and most failures in proper flowering may be attributed to this cause.
-The pinnts, if rooted in pot's, maybe kept )ver the winter, and no harm results in planting n the spring direct from the pots, without dis- mrbing the roots.

div.head: IRIS.
div.p: THE IRIS.

Irises are to be found`growing in their wild state in almost every country. Tht. varieties have been so much improved by hybridists that it now possible to secure flpWers from March to October. Some of the irises. have a commer: cial value. Iris florentina, with its white or. pale blue flowers, found irr abundance in Southern Europe, is grown to produce the violet-scented' orris root so largely used in perfumery, while the seeds of iris pseudacorus have been used as an excellent substitute for coffee, the flavour Of the roasted berry being very .similar. From iris florentina is extracted a pigment called ver-
dillis or iris green, which is used by miniature painters. There are quite a large number of varieties and it is an easy matter to raise good fine plants from seed.

div.head: LILY OF THE VALLEY.
div.p: LILY OF THE VALLEY.

In some gardens this univeisally admired flower grows like a weed. If a small portion happens. to become detached from the parent , root it quickly takes hold and comes up in un- expected places. . There are, again, other- gar- dens where the greatest difficulty is experienced in getting it to grow at all. Position, of course, has a lot to do with its successful culture, and a shady mid-day spot should be Chosen. A south border. is best for early flowering. When established in a suitable soil they quickly be- come crowded by the production of .shoots, which, become- more numerous year by year.. All these tend to impoverish the older flowering • crowns by competing with them for nourish- ment. To have large flowers new plantations ' should be made every four Years, breaking up the crowns and 'planting the largest by them- selves, the next -size alone, and the smallest together. It is not advisable to break up the whole of the bed at once, but to treat a por- tion each year, as there will be only a scant supply of flowers got from file disturbed plants the first year, no matter how 'good the crowns are or how well planted. By treating the bed in sections a good supply of flowers may be maintained.

div.head: IN THE POULTRY PEN.
div.p: IN THE POULTRY PEN.

It is well to remember the value of meat as an egg-producer, and with regard to the various ingredients of the daily food there is nothing vetter in the way Of soft stuff than scalded bis- cuit meal dried off with sharps, pea-meal and Vi heat, unfortunately, is rather dear for poultry just at present, but a good se- lection can. be made from plump white oats, dari, white peas and maize. The latter is essen- tially a winter grain, being heating and -fatten- ing, and for hens that are running in compara- tive liberty it may be given in fair • quantities, though fowls in small runs do not need so much, and should not have more than one part Maize with. three parts of -other grain, such as oats and dui.
KILLING A CHICKEN.

Whatever be the method of killing—ad • it 1 does not matter a greal deal how it is done-- see that it, is done expeditiously. It is, how- ever. absolutely imperative that, Whichever method of killing is adopted, the head is kept hanging downwards until all the blood has left the body, or drained into the neck at the base of the skull. Unless this is done, the flesh is dark in colour, which further detracts from the bird's appearance. Immediately after the bird '1 is killed plueldrig should be commenced. If this - • is done when the body is warm the dan6.4 1 tearing the skin is ruirhuttsul. •

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1913.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1913.
FAMILY ; INCOME 24/8-12.
Problem of Granting Exemption before School Age Expires.
ILLUMINATING DISCUSSION.

A sad tale of a family of nine _struggling to subsist on 245. fild. a .week was 'narrated during a discussion on the question of granting exemp- tions to scholars under school age at a meeting of the Warrington Education Committee on Monday evening. The School Attendance Sub- committee reported that 116 exemptions had been granted during the past month. Mr. J. 'UPSON protested against the granting of exemptions wholesale. There were during the month 119 applications and 116 had been granted exemptions. He thought the sub-com- mittee-should exercise greater care. There were 119 cases to be investigated in one afternoon, and that number could not be investigated properly in that time. In one case exempted during the past month, the father of the boy was a trades- man earning a 'Minimum Wage of 30s. per week, and two boys were earning Bs. and 10s. per week respectively. The parents also had a shop, and the boy now exempted had been engaged selling newspapers morning, noon and night. .Fre- quently the boy was so overcome, by the work that he often fell sound asle'ep in school. The parents had exploited the boy for years, until he was a dwarf, much below the usual height and weight. Although he should have been medically examined on three occasions, he had evaded the examination every time. When the parents knew the doctor was to attend the school, the boy was kept away. He maintained that there had not been sufficient investigation of the case before exemption was granted.

div.head: Wilberforce Wanted..
div.p: A Wilberforce Wanted..

We want, said Mr. Upson, another Wilber- force to lead a campaign, not against the non- enslavement of the black, but against the non- enslavement of the white child. I think we ought to press the question of raising school age. and see that our by-laws are properly adminis- tered.

Mr. JARMAN said .Mr. Upson seemed to have got more information about the case than was before the committee. There would always be false statements regarding the wages, for it was not always possible to get at the income. Mr. C. E. PARKER raised the subject of blind alley occupations, and asked if it was a rule for the committee to refuse exemvtion to children into such occupations. Was it not a case that many authorities made it a definite rule that unless a child went into some occupation that would lead to something in the future the ex enytion was refund?

Family of Nine and £1 4s. gid. per week. Councillor IIENSHALL knew of the case of a family of nine with a total income of £1 48. 81d. per week, where exemption had been refused because there was no necessity. Pr4ably Mr. Upson's Wilberforce would have something to say about such a case. Mr. UPSON : Such a case has not occurred dur- ing the past month? Councillor HENSHALL said it did occur recently. The father earned ..tl, a boy 4s. 80., and in the family was a child three. month's old, and yet exemption was ref tmd on the ground that there was no necessity. roore were a great number of the 119 cases obviously cases of necessity, and it was so obvious there WitS no need to inter- view the parents on that point. It might be that in the committee's anxiety to consider the 'needs of- the parent they went further than Mr. Upson thought they ought to go. The difficulty was to define what was really a necessitous case.
If there was no probability of the child being properly fed while at school, it was much better to let it go to work and earn something towards its keep.

div.head: Guardians Could Not Give Relief.
div.p: Guardians Could Not Give Relief.
They had been told they should not perform the duty of the relieving committee. Suppose such a child went to the auardians, they could not relieve it with their limited powers, and

the position the School Attendance Committee was in was: if they refused exemption because there was no necessity, the Guardians would• be bound to refuse on the same grounds: If the compait4should len to anything it should be to mercy's side. Mr. UPSON : It is not merciful to the child.

_ Councillor HENRIALL : Feed the brain and starve the child seems to be Mr. Upson's view. Mr. VPSON : I am not quarrelling with neces- sitous cases. Councillor HENSHALL : Then the question is: What is necessity? Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH held there should be no exemptions given until a child had been ex- amined by the medical officer. That principle should be adopted.

Examination and Income. Alderman JAMES EvANs : I cannot agree with Mr. Fairclough on that point. There does not seem to be any connection 'between the medical officer and the income. Mr. FAIRCLOUGH : There is a medical officer ap- pointed to examine every child in the town, and I think a certificate should he given before a child can be exempted. Mr. G. WALKER thought it was little use keep- ing a child in school until the age of 14 when it could not do the work of the fourth standard. . Councillor PEMBERTON thought it was more im- portant to the working class that they should have a frame of 'vigour rather than a great edu- cation. Much had been made of cul-de-sac em- ployment, but it was easy for a boy to get out of that. It depended upon himself whether he would get out or stay in. Mr. E. PLINSTON said that every case was as strictly investigated as possible. Finally the matter dropped.

div.head: RIVAL COMMITTEES.
div.p: RIVAL COMMITTEES.
The Squabble Over Appointment of
a School Nurse.
A CONFERENCE PROPOSED

The squabble over who should appoint a school nurse was carried a further stage at the Education Committee meeting on Monday evening. This Committee recommended to the last meeting of the Council that such a nurse should be appointed. The Health Committee objected to this act on the part of the educa- tionists, on the ground that the Education Com- mittee were assuming to itself what was the duty of the Health Committee, and after a lively debate. Councillor H. Roberts withdrew the recommendation, which came once- more before the Education Committee, over whom Councillor Roberts presided. Mr. J. UPsaN, referring to the. Town Council's attitude, said the time had come when the matter should be thrashed out. The position was: The Medical Officer was elected. by the Council, and to his salary the Education Com- mittee contributed ...t5O a year; .the Assistant Medical Officer had his salary paid by the Com- mittee, and in his appointment the Committe<, had no voice, and in that the Health Com- mittee might have properly sought co-opera- tion. While the Health Committee was con- cerned with the general health, the Education Committee were most concerned with the health of the school children, and in the case of thn nurse it was not a new office they were creating. but simply making an appointment to an exist- ing office.

div.head: Friction Between Committees.
div.p: Friction Between Committees.

The time had come when some means should I be- devised to cause the friction between the. two committees to cease. The procedure was clumsy and the position _illogical, . and the Council ought to realise that it was impossible , to continue upon existing lines. The position was unique. There they had the Medical In- spection Sub-committee doing work and paying the salaries of those who did the work, and yet .another body made the appointments. He did not think such a thing obtained in connection, with any other committee, and Sir George New- man told the Education Committee deputation to the-Board.of Education that in no other town in England was such a procedure athipted. • The Education Committee . did. not want to exercise any patronage or -fill a 'position for the sake of making an appointment; they wanted' to do so because of their specialised knowledge of the work, which enabled them to make a better appointment than could the Health Com- mittee. There were several courses open to the Educatir.in comn.littee he tih tha: best - Would be to ask the General Purposes Committee, which was the Council, to receive a deputation to discuss the Matter and arrive at a method whereby the difficulty could be removed. He moved that.

div.head: No Friction Desired.
div.p: No Friction Desired.

Councillor PEMBERTON thought, first of all, th‘l committee should re-pass the resolution, and send it back to the Council. Such a course would make it easier. for them to meet the General Purposes Committee. He did not think ,there would be the. slightest friction, unless•the Education Committee caused it. The Town Council nor the Health Committee had the slightest wish to cause friction, and no thought the Town Council were right and proper in desiring to keep all appointments in its own hands.

Alderman JAMES EVANS, chairman of the Health Committee, said he did not .approach ;the subject in any spirit of antagonism. The 'Health Committee from time to time had been accused of doing what they bad never done, and he heard such remarks madela public, and such were made at the Guild of Help meeting in that room only last week.

div.head: "Austere or Domineering."
div.p: "Austere or Domineering."

It was said the ifealth Committee had assumed an austere or domineering attitude to the 31e1ical Inspection Sub-committee. They had not, and the Health Co 2,rai-ace had always acted towards them on gen üs lines and'had always sought for cohesion and co-operation. They had never assumed an attitude of dicta- tion and he protested against the hard things -and had been said about the antagonistic feel- ing of the Health Committee. Mr. JARMAN said Councillor Pemberton and Alderman Evans were present at the School Melical Inspection •Committee when the reso- lution was first proposed—(Alderman Evans: I was, not, sir)—and surely if it was against the Council's Minutes- they could then have ri.ised objection instead of allowing the matter to 'go to the Council. He had heard it said there 1% its nothing to confer about. Alderman JAMES EVANS : I have never said so, and Mr. Jarman is. not justified in bringing in such a remark. -

div.head: No Slight Intended.
div.p: No Slight Intended.

Mr. C. E. PARKER. thought they should get to know the principle by -which the Medical In- 'spection Sub-:committee were to be guided in such matters. The matter of the appointment of a nurse Was in their hands and no slight was intended upon the Health Committee. They appointed the lady who it was intended to re- place, and naturally the Medical Inspc..ion Sub-committee, thought they were right to Pro- ceed.with the proposed appointment. No slight had been introduced from their side.

(Ifear, hear.) It seemed strange that when sub-committees of the Education Committee appointed officers, from headmasters -downwards, they were told they must not make an appointment in that case. He thought the position now taken up was most erratic, and ft was an unreasonable position far any committee to be put in.

div.head: Wanted Cohesion.
div.p: Wanted Cohesion.
Mr. •PLINSTON hoped. Alderman ,Evans was sincere when he said he wanted cohesion. He did not know what the Health Committee had to dread and fear. - _

Mr. UPSON said if Alderman Evans and Coun- cillor Pemberton would promise to get a con- ference between the General Purposes Com- mittee and the Medical Inspection Sub-com- mittee he would accept that as a solution. CoUncillor ROBERTS, the chairman, thought that the preferable course. They were ex- tremely anxious to avoid any apparent frktion.. The Health Committee was practically a sub- committee of the Council, and it seemed illogical for one committee to dictate to an- other as to the appointment of an officer who would be paid by the Education Committee. Finally Mr. UPsoN withdrew his resolution on the understanding that a conference, would be arranged.

div.head: FOUGHT AT LUCKNOW.
div.p: FOUGHT AT LUCKNOW.

The funeral of the late John Potter, believed to be the last of Macclesfield's Indian Mutiny veterans, took place at the borough cemetery on Saturday, with military honours. Potter, who was 78 years of age, joined the 64th Regiment of Foot. in May, 1852, and was With Sir Henry Havelock's relief force which marched from Cal- cutta to Lucknow. During the siege of Luck- now, he was shot through the jaw whilst saving the life of a comrade, Joseph Albinson, another Macclesfield man, Who died some years ago. Sub- sequently Potter received a sabre wound in the thfoat, and later, whilst fighting at the gates of Lucknow, had his right hand- shot, necessitat- ing the amputation of the limb.

div.head: WOMEN'S QUESTINS.
div.p: WOMEN'S QUESTINS.
Feathers Higher and Higher—Hats
Smaller and Smaller.
ROYALTY AND WOMEN RIDERS.

The King and Queen strongly disapprove of ilie cross-saddle for woinen riders.. His Majesty has on more than one occasion ex- pressed his opinion to this effect, and as might have been - expected, Princess -Mary used the conventional side-saddle when the other day she made her first appearance in the hunting field at a meet of the West • Norfolk Hounds. There never was any sufficient 'reason for women -abandoning the side-saddle. The new Tflode bectime popular mainly from the love of lovelty and spirit of change, which are such eonspicuous _features of modern life. The old Style is infinitely more -graceful, and as to the belief in the greater safety of the cross-saddle, experience has shown it to be a myth. Many expert lady riders have been giving their views on this subject in one of the ladies' journals. and the general opinion is that the side-saddle is mori graceful and safer than the cross seat. The vogue for the new mode may, after all, be only a- passing one. - •
Amusing Parties.

Afternoon parties used to be considered dull, insipid and dowdy, but the Tango has altered all that, and these ,functions are now not only smart, but amusing. Dancing is by no means their only attraction. Palmistry, and Other mysteries are indulged in, and bridge has of late taken the place of the Tango in some houses. The old-fashioned sit-down tea has been revived, and such solid comestibles as ham, toast, and poached eggs, now appear as a Matter of course. Of sandwiches there is no end, and their variety is ,infinite. Hot cakes of all kinds and sorts, with home-made Scones, are a feature of the feast, whilst rich fruit, tipsy and other cakes, abound, with sweets of all kinds. Nor are the guests who may be doing diet cures forgotten, and for their delectation, dry toast, lemonade, Milk, cream, and sacchar- ine instead of sugar, are provided. A new idea that meets a want are the pretty silver sand- wich tongs, that Make a useful and somewhat novel wedding present.

Floral Muffs. The muff of real flowers was a summer inven- tion that died almost as soon as it was brought :lit, but in COnsevence of the present glut of flowers—due probagly to the extremely mild autumn—it has been revived, and bids fair to be the favourite bouquet for the Christmas season and for Christmas gifts. Brides have favoured the irle;,t (Wring the 1(1,5,t fortnight, and a muff of snow white orchids is exdingly lovely. In London, floral muffs have been worn at the Tango teas, that are a feature of the littleseasons' "functions. Many of these were magnificent, more especially those made of chrysanthemums, and in size the floral muff is of mammoth proportions, except when worn by very yOung girls, and then medium or quite small ones are carried. The back of the muff may be of flowers, foliage, or the 'satin or gauze that holds the flowers in place. The work can only be successfully parried out by trained -workers, as the utmost delicacy and lightness is required in handling the blossoms.

The Feminine Note in Tailor-mades. Last spring.there was a tendency on the part of fashionable tnilors,to adopt masculine modes as far as possible to the tailor-made coat and skirt.. This winter a change has set in—An the opposite direction. There is a distinctly femin- ine note in this autumn's styles, and after the turn of the year this note will be much more strongly emphasised. The change is ascribed to VilriOUS causes, for the whims of La Mode are •PCA always acccti..j.nted,.4or. propably the fact ,that.women‘are employed as tailoresses in much larger numbers than ever before, and-that they have introduced the many feminine touches, is the likeliegt explanation. At any rate the cos- tumes. prepared for the liivierw—and these generally show the tendency for early spring modes—lean not at all to the masculine, but are provided with dainty coats of the bolera type. With these are worn absolutely shapeless vests :! of coarse linen, with high standing collars. The coats are somewhat pouched. ,

A New Hat MaterfaL. Higher ,and -higher are the feathers, and smaller and smaller the hats. The latest fan- tasy in mounts resembles an mnbrella or rather a parasol. The frondlesS stein forms the handle, a rounded cluster of fronds the parascl and the point above is crowned_ with a ferrule. Manufacturers have already decided 'on the straw's, and styles for next summer's hats, and from Luton conies the announcement that a new and inexpensive material, which closely re- sembles straw, and is a perfect imitation of Panama, has been inucnted. It is bleached in its raw state; and is quite white, but neither the sun nor the air causes it to turn colour; nor is _it affected by rain. IV is made in white and tussore shades only, at. least at present. The process of making, and the material- of which these hats are made • iS4 a trade secret.

The Jersey and the Ratty Sash. Paris has revived the cosy and becoming jersey, which has not been seen over here for a very long time, but will doubtless now be very soon in evidence. It was worn a great deal last suininer in the country, but as it is practical and useful, especially for the hotise, it has been made in woven silks—that have the appearance of being closely knitted-for winter wear.. The brightest fa-lyrist colours are chosen, .such as cherry, emerald green, and bright shades of. blue. Belts of patent and other -leather are worn with it, and in some cases butt Ons are the only adornment, and these are of any of the semi-precious stones. The sash becomes every day a more prominent feature, and a novelty that deserves mention is the short baby sash of nursery type, which has been introduced by tailors orr their latest models._ It proceeds from the side seams of the coat, and is tied at the back in a bow with very short ends. Side sagfies are seen on all the new evening gowns. They generally have huge bows to the shoulders, and long ends, and re- quire careful adjusting.
HOW I RUBBED AWAY A STONE OF FAT-FROM MY HIPS AND
ABDOMEN IN TWO WEEKS TIME

For yers I tried every possible means to hide the excessive fat On my hips and abdomen; it seemed as if it had accumulated on just the two places that it would be most noticeable. Everything that I tried failed to make me any thinner. But thanks to a lady friend who had studied herboristerie, I learned- the secret of a harmless plan which enabled me to rub away with ease a stone of ,useless fat in only two weeks. The plan is so simple and some of my friends , seem so glad•to know of it that I think there may be sister readers of the Warrington "Examiner" who have perhaps been longing for this very advice. First, get from any good chemist 1 dram of quassia chips and 3 ounces of cirola hark extract. Take them home and after putting the quassia chips in a pan pour over it ' a teacupful of boiling water. When this has ' stood for about a minute, strain through a cloth and add the cirola bark extract. Then pour the mixture into a bottle and apply it every night :and morning with your hands P)r about ten minutes, using a circular movement. Each time you can almost see some of the fat melt away. At first -I thought it must be a. dream, but when I measured there was no longer any doubt. I soon grew too slender for my clothes, and had to have them taken in, but it was -a pleasure to do, it. and f shall feel eternally grateful to the lady who ehoweil me how easy it I was to regain my youthful figure. E. L. A.

div.head: SOLDIER'S FRIEND.
div.p: THE SOLDIER'S FRIEND.
Warringtonian's Work In !ndia.

The foundation-stone of the new Army Branch Buildings of the Young Men'S Christian Asso- ciation was laid at Bangalore by the Viceroy of India, to whom an address was presented, on behalf of the local committee, by the Rev. Joseph Callan, the general secretary, and a Warringtonian, setting for in detail the past and prospective work of the Y.M.C..A. In his reply, the Viceroy said: "I have heard a ge--11 deal of the work done by Mr. Callan among the troops, especially in camp, and I feel confident that you have in him a man excepOonally well qualified to give effect to the general scheme of this institution, which , will, with the benefit of his guidance, com- mence its career under the happiest auspices. I hope and believe that the ceremony which I am now about to perform may be symbolical of a great step forward in making the life of our soldiers more happy and more useful, alike for themselves and thAr country." _ _

•Mr. Callan was formerly a boy in the Sunday School belonging to Emmanuel Reformed •Epis- copal Church, Warrington, when that .school- was located at Arpley Station. Ho was then an apprentice to the iron-moulding trade at the Pearson and Knowles' iron works. His desire to become a missionary was encouraged and fostered by the Rev. Edward T. Reed, a former minister of Emmanuel Church, who Stood by Mr. Callan while he was a student at Cheshunt College, where he passed with credit, through the whole five years' course of training; after- wards taking a six months' course in elemen- tary medicine, &c., at Livingstone College; Ley- tonstone. During his furlough, about two years ago, Mr. Callan took by examination • the degree of Bachelor of Divinity at 'Hartford Theological Seminary, United States. He is now engaged in a work of far-reaching importance at Bangalore, both for native.young men, and also for those in the British Army;' indeed, he was recently described by an English officer out there as one of the best friends the British soldier had ever had in India.
