div.head: `Ci HAPPY cnosTmas EVE.
div.p: `Ci HAPPY cnosTmas EVE.
How a Legal
Hampden.
Dispute was Settled by a Village

In the village the squire did not count. He was an absentee landlord, seen of us only in the shooting season. In the case of his local agent, it was an entirely different matter. A keen man of business, born and bred in the district, he knew the place and people " throo threed to needle," as the .old wives said. And this know- ledge was of inestimable advantage to the squire; his master.

'Timmy o' Dooaz's " himself ultimately yielded to the. blandishmeuts .of the squire'z . . astute representative and what a'fall Was that!! For Timmy, one of the last of the old hand- loom weavers, had always led those who from time to time ventured to withstand the steward to his face. One morning the villagers awoke to the start- ling fad that a- privilege they had enjoyed for innumerable generations had been withdrawn. Timmy's call to arms was promptly obeyed by the bulk of the male population. There was • a terrible -display of wrath, and it was unanimously resolved- that. there 'should be a fight to a' finish. Timmy over- ruled/ a'n impetuous demand for a demonstra- tion, suggesting instead certain legal proceeding which were bound to have a favourable issue. Upon this he was prepared to stake ,his established repu- tation as hedge-lawyer; moreover, he undertook personally to conduct the case in court, with the reasonable stipulation that his so indignant and apparently not less determined neighbours should then and there pledge themselves to supply the -wherewithal. Three did so; the Hothers required a little time for consideration, and for their convenience the meeting was ad- journed for four-and-twenty houils. On re-assembling, such .of the latter.as put. in an appearance began with one consent to make 'excuse, and only the three, first individuals re- mained faithful:' .After a while .even these be- came alarmed by the prospect of a strUggle against the wealthy landowner over the Uncer- tainties of the law; and ere long Timmy alone was found steadfast. Besides, his wife and daughter having no sympathy whatever With his disinterested efforts in behalf of the com- munity. his greatest foes in a real sense were those of his own household. From the first they held that of all the hare-brained' enterprises and forlorn hopes with which he had been prominently associated, this latest was tht most 014444444+014014444444 44.14 44 4444+ q4i4 44+,14'

div.head: CHRISTMAS BEER.
div.p: CHRISTMAS BEER.
Workhouge Inmates Festive Pints Are Now Ensured.

div.head: EXTRA FOR OUTDOOR POOR.
div.p: EXTRA FOR OUTDOOR POOR.

There is joy at the Warrington Workhouse. The beer for the Christmas festivities, which was threatened to be kept locked, bolted and barred, out of the‘way of the inmates, is now to flow in brimful pints on Christmas Day, and the alarm, which-the notice of /notion, given by Mrs. Simpson, to "stop that beer" can now subside, as the motion has been withdrawn and the beer will be there. •

By the casting vote of, the Chairinan, Mr. E. L. Bent, at the Guardians' meeting on Wednes- day, the initdoor poor will have t 'chance to Make merry as well at the festive season, for now each adult will receive is. 6d. extra, and each child 9d. extra to mark th 3 occasion. It was the Rev. A. M. Mitchell who played so effectively the part of Santa Claus and secured the gift for the outdoor poor, but he had to fight hard to secure it, as was shown by the necessity of the Chairman giving his .casting vote in favour of the extra pay.

div.head: Anti-beer Motion Withdrawn
div.p: Anti-beer Motion Withdrawn
When the meeting came to the motion, given notice of, to stop - the Christmas beer at the Workhouse feast, Mrs. SIMPSON announced that she would withdraw, it.. •

I withdraw the Motion, she said, not because I .am afraid of defeat, but because of come of the remarks by members of the Board of Guar- dians, which led flie, to see-that their minds were still in the beer. (Laughter.) You men are so constituted as not to be easily led to give up (A .Member, sotto voice: "Beer ")—what you consider a good old custom. I hope the pre- sent, or the next, .generation will not be afraid to depart from some of their ways .of .error. (Laughter.) The Board approved of the motion being with- drawn.
The Ev. A. M. :MITCHELL -Tose to propoFo a resolution.
Mr. FURNESS : I propose you follow suit to Mrs. Simpson.
MT. MITCHELL: Pm not prepared to do that.
For the Outdoor Poor.

Mr. MITCHELL moved that the minute refu4ing, a Christmas allowance of is. 6d. to adults in receipt -of out relief and 9d. to each child be rescinded and the allowance granted. He contended .that if they could entrust the out•reliefers with a -ftlitrly large sum per week, surely they • could trust them with a gratuity amounting to is. 6d. It was a libel on these poor to say they would misuse that money. They had .made special arrangements for the inmates, and it was inconsistent to give the inmates Of the House that and give. nogratuity to the out- reliefers: The cost would be only about and that would not affect the rates to a fraction of a: half-penny. It was a question of .discrini- illation, and it was absurd .to 'say they could discriminate between the good and the bad. Although there was not the same amount of expansive waistcoats shown by the Guardians that day he hoped they would agree to giving the gratuity. Mr. F. MCKINLEY seconded.

div.head: An Inconsistent Action.
div.p: An Inconsistent Action.

Mr. T. DALE said those in receipt of outdoor relief should have as much consideration as those inside the House. These people were in the bare of the Guardians as much'as the -in- mates of the House. (Hear, hear.) Other unions were Paying extra through their officials, and it was inconsistent that their own out-poor should not get anything. Many of the cases outside were most deserving people, more deserv- ing, he thought, than were some Of the inmates of the Workhouse. (Hear, • hear.) Some -other. Guardians were giving 25., while the Warring-. ten sugge,stion was is. 6d. I do not think, he concluded, there is a rate-. payer in the Warrington Union who would like to sit down to his Christmas - fare with the thought that there was a, poor family in; the Union who had been neglected; .(Hear, heir.) Mr. W. C. 111,0011i4 said they; as a Board, should not be inconsistent: The -proposal had already been defeated, and now the minority were in- consistent in seeking to snatch a victory. Mr. MclimEr I Don't you think that.
Mr. A. J. Jolley Strongly Objects. Mr. A. J. jougr strongly oblected to the ro-

div.head: BY A. O. J.
div.p: BY A. O. J.

desperate and foolish. While yet he had some sort of backing, they taunted him with being " cat's-paw as usual "; and when his disciples forsoolc, him and lied, they Worried him with 'dismal prognostications :Of disaster, ' with the " bastile " as tile only possible end. In vain did the harassed Timmy, what time he could get a word in edgeways, protest that failure was in this instance utterly impossible. His wife, gen- uinely afraid lest they should be "sold up stick an' stump," and lashed to fury by Timmy's seeming indifference and stupidity, assailed him with such torrents of abuse that he was fain p seek-ref-age 'elsewhere. .'kAll-the same :he adhered to his deterraination to Prosecute his suit against the squire. . Perceiving- which, and knowing well his Man, the steward' addressed to Timmy a curt note ask- ing the old fellow to meet him at the principal hotel in the -market town on .the following Wednesday, December 24th. Upon this ensued more domestic trouble, the two women seeing in it the impending crisis which was to overwhelm and sweep them into the dreaded poorhouse, and railing the more at the imperturbable Timmy. Punctual at the interview, the hitter was effu- sively welcomed by the smiling steward. After a delightful hour's small talk, &c., &c. (particu- larly et beteras), the man of business adroitly passed to the dispute in question. He assured his " great and oldest friend" that the change which the -squire proposed would not deprive Timmy of his ancient ric,hts-. As for the rest, be went on to urge, why should so Worthy and honest, but admittedly , poor a man eh- danger his own interests, especially the -peace and happiness' of his family, by persistence in a lawsuit which would bring him neither honour nor profit, but in all likelihood the contrary? ..And to this and much more to the like effect the tempter added that, while of course all thought of bribery was out of the .question, if Timmy could see his way to accept by Way of tribute from a humble admirer a cheque for £lO3 from a book 'which lay on the table before him, nothing would give the speaker greater pleasure than to draw it at once. Timmy hesitated, demurred, argued, _and at -length yielded—on the .distinct understanding, however, that the gift was purely an honorarium —and that for the .cheque there should be sub- stituted one hundred golden sovereigns in a bag. When on that Memorable Christmas Eve Timmy reached his cottage, soaked to the skin —for rain had fallen heavily during his, long tramp—he had a reception which may well be described as chilling. On one side of the fire- place sat his daughter, reading a paper which

lay open on her knee, and from which she did not for a moment raise her eyes. On the oppo- site side her mother rocked herself and moaned. There were no signs of preparation for a meal, Timmy divested himself of his' wet upper gar- ment without a word. Then walking up to the empty table, he poured upon it the contents of his precious bag. The girl was too engrossed in her Christmas story to notice the extraordinary turn of events. The old woman,. by no means 'so pre-occupied, experienced a strange conflict of emotions. At first dumb with amazenient at the sight of such Wealth, she soon covered suffi- Ciently to ask in .an awe-stricken whisper if it Meant that the Misguided and miserable being to whom it was her misfortune to be tied for life had, in addition to his previous follies and sins, committed the crime of highway robbery. Timmy, likewise speaking in an undertone, briefly explained the situation as altered by implied arrangement with the steward. Imme- diately on realising the true state of affairs, the wife turned upon the still unsuspecting daugh- ter, and, giving that astonished damsel a vigorous and unwonted shaking, indulged in another characteristic tirade. "However can thou fashion an' find i' thi' heart?" demanded she; " sittie theer all ov 'a lump at this time o' day, an' till poor owd feyther, worth a scoor o' sich like, fit to catch his death o' cowd throo bein' out i' all 1;11174-Wild weather, an' havin' nowt i' his inside., Stir thee this minute, madam, before I gi' thee a hidin' as thou desarves. Some fowk doesn't know when they have a good feyther; an' I'll ha' thee to know 'at he's one i' a thousand is thine. I allus did say .'at I'd wed one o' th' best fellies ivver walked, an' he knows I think weel on hinr whether his child does or not. As for youd chaps 'at left him to feight his battle • wi' th' squire, an' nub'dy but Me to say a en- couragin' word to him, ther isn't th' odd- 'lan 'at's fit to holl'd a cannel to him. I knew all -th' time 'at- he had his heead screwed on th' reight..roStl, an' -'at we should' be a deeal better an' not war off. throo :this • law job. What's th' lass starin' theer like a stuck sheep for i'stead o'.gerrin' th' kettle on for his teen't .But I. see plainly 'at I shall la' to do for ' Lu mysen if o*t is done. Gooa thi ways, lad, an' ,get • them sypin' breeches 'dOfft. I've p-i; thi slippers to warm, sithi ; an' i' ten Minutes or a quarter ow an hour I'll ha' thi Sich a blow out as nub'dy else could gi' thi. We've' had ours, an' thine would 'a been ready waitin' fat.: thi but I couldn't tell just when to expect 'thi." Timmy was supposed to .swallow this along with his "high tea." Anyhow it was a happy Christmas Eve.

div.head: Remarkable St. Helens Treasure.
div.p: Remarkable St. Helens Treasure.
Trove Case.
INQUEST ON BAG OF COLD.

A unique experience befel Coroner Brighouse at St. Helens on Tuesday. Although holding the coronership for 30 years, it was the first time he was called upon to hold an inqiiest on a bag of gold.. The sum which was found by two boys amounted to £l5l 10s. The claimants for the money were the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster; Colonel W. Lee Pilkington, lord of the manor of Sutton, and the St. Helens Co- operative Society. All these parties made claims to the money, while a claim was also entered by the United Alkali Company. The coroner 'said ,an Act of Parliament as far back as 1276 directed the coroner to hold an in- quiry in all cases of- treasurertrove, and by the Coroners Act of 1887 that jurisdiction was specially preserved. He referred to the law on the subject, and reminded the jury that treas- ure-trove consisted of gold -or silver advertently deposited anywhere without abandonment, the owner being unknown. Reginald- and "William Thomas, schoolboys, stated,that they were on their ivay to school on November 20, and when crossing some waste land behind Herbert-street they noticed a littlel bag in a hollow in the ground, with a grass sod near, which looked as if it had just been pulled off. ,They found the bag was full of sovereigns, and after giving three of their companions a sovereign each,' they took it home, where they handed it over. to Mrs. Lievesley, who was nurs- ing their mother. She took the money upstairs, and commenced to count it, but when "she got to, forty Mrs'. Thomas said: "Stop.; it is excit- ing me." (Laughter.)'

The Chief Constable said there Were 151 sov- ereigns, which were all Victorian, and one half- :sovereign, which was an Edward, dated 1906. The jury fund that the money had been found by the boys and that it was treasure-trove.- The Coroner intimated that he would hold the money until the claimants had fought out their right to it, and then he would hand it Over.

div.head: MAYOR AND THE P.S.A.
div.p: MAYOR AND THE P.S.A.

The Mayor, .Councillor Peacock, presided at the open meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. on Sunday afternoon. He said he highly valued the expression of goodwill sent by the members of the brotherhood when he was elected as Mayor. He was glad to tell them that the Council were now doing all they could to im- prove the dwellings of the -poor and the en- vironments Which surrounded the poor.

- • - The Council, he might say, were always ready to receive advice and counsel from any rate- payer in the town, ,and he thought they were shoWing.a Christian spirit in their endeavour to improve the position of the tramway men on the Lord's Day, and -the scheme was to give the men every alternate Sunday off duty. They were also trying to get free rides on the trams. They were also endeavouring to do something for the children between the, ages of one and five, so that the child in the lowest posikion should have the health afforded to the child‘in the highest state.

'Mr. Martindale, Wilmslow, spoke on the les- sons learned from the Good Samaritan. He was satisfied that the world was better now than it was 100 years ago. At one time P.S.A. work was looked upon as contrary to the ideals of the chureh, but, he thoiight,. they had lived down that idea.-

Mr. and Mrs. J. Sephton sang nicely the duet "Watchman, what of the nighT. Mrs. Seph- ton rendered "Abide with me," and Mr. Seph- ,ton "Nearer, my God, to Thee." Mr. Payton presided at the organ with his customary ability. Messrs. 11. Osborne and B. Farrar (secretary) also took .part in the meeting. Two new mem- bers were given a hearty welcome,' and .the Secretary proposed that a 'message of congratu- lation be sent to Mr. • and Mrs. A. Tilling. of Lower Walton, on the celebration of their golden Wedding.

div.head: WORLD'S TRIBUTE FOR OUR TABLE.
div.p: WORLD'S TRIBUTE FOR OUR TABLE.
Age cannot wither, nor custom stale, their infinite varietY•
"Now Christmas is come, Let us beat up the drum, And call all our neighbours together; And when they appear, Let us make them such cheer, As will keep out the wind and the weather."

This week we are a little bit nearer our Christ- mas dinner, but before we are ushered into this banqueting • scene we must still pay a visit to some of our local shops, which are Ricrowtled now with Christmas cheer. We will just take a peep into GROCERIES AND PROVISIONS. .

Among the grocers and provision merchants into whose establishments we have taken ,a peep this . week are those of Messrs„ Henry Stilling and Co., Horsemarket-street ; Messrs. Wm. Owen and Sons, Sankey-street; Messrs. Lipton Ltd., Bridge-street; 'Messrs. Wm. Monks and Son, Ltd., Bridge-street; Mr. Peter Leigh, Horsemarket- street ; Messrs. J. Povey and Son, Bridge-street; Messrs.. J. B. Isaac and Co., Sankey-street; Messrs. Ben,Few and Son, Winwick-street ; and Mr. Arthur Clowes, Horsemarket-street. - Messrs. Milling and Co. give a choice of all kinds of dainties for Christmas. Apples, New: town pippins, for dessert; almonds, biscuits, chocolates, crackers, Chinese figs, dates, Finland fruits, filberts, nuts, oranges, Turkish delight, shortbread, plum puddings, glace cherries., grapes (English and foreign), hams, bacon, butter, and tea in fancy tins, Mazipans, which are delightful and delicious in all kinds of choice caskets. These make most suitable presents for Christmas, and are certainly very acceptable to all who are fortunate enough to redeive them. In Messrs. Owen and Sons' well-stocked em- porium we find all kinds of delicacies ready for the festive season. I think everybody is remem- bered. The children can be well Supplied with stockings- filled with goody-goodies, sets of -tiny furniture and tea sets (no doubt each article crammed with bon-bons), Christmas trees, and Japanese, toys of every description to hang thereon, flowers for table decoration, ginger wines and non-alcoholic drinks, mincemeat, dates, jellies, tempting bottles of filets.d'anchois a l'huile d'olive, French articles of musical fame. You can have a clothes brush which will play you a tune whilst brushing the dust from your coat, or you can have a German drinking cup which will regale you with a lively tune whilst you are dining. Home-made plum pud- dings and crackers, beside the ordinary stock of groceries, meet our eyes on every_ side, Lipton's •are proprietors of many estates in Ceylon, which produce their famous teas, coffees and cocoas.. They have also a fine stock of fancy cakes, shortbreads, jams, marmalades, bacon, hams, and things for Christmas, such as plum puddings, raisins, currants, sugars, and a never- ending supply of eggs. They also make np,com- bination parcels of their best goods, which make very suitable Christmas gifts for rich and poor alike.

Messrs. Monks and Son have a fine, show of groceries for Christmas. We can choose our cakes for our Christmas tea from a variety of shapes and .sizes. We can have one nicely- decorated. with holly, looking quite delicious on its bed of ice," or we can take one looking- quite toothsome without -its - layer of icing. Turkish delight, Loncoums figs, dessert fruits, nuts from far-away Brazil or sunny Spain. The invalids are not forgotten, for we can stock, them up with a bottle or two of Junora, Win- carnis or Vibrona, every drop of which is guar- anteed to brace them. up for the January days, which are soon to come upon us.- In the shop over the way we can get home-made bread, butter, cheese, eggs, and all kinds of dairy pro- duce.- _ _ _ _ _ _

The old-established business of Mr. Peter Leigh still keeps up its reputation for supplying its customers with the best. They have a good supply of groceries of every description, all the necessities for making plum- puddings, mince pies, and those table delicacies which are within the reach of all.

In Sankey-street Messrs. Isaac and Co. have a fine stock of special Christmas hams, Wilt- shire bacon, cheeses of every kind, from Stilton, Cheshire and cream cheese to cheese Which should be served hot on toast. Dried fruits, lemon peel, citron, spices, tinned fruits, such as peaches "still in their 'bloom," pears, apples; apricots and "pines," NOT exactly the sort they grow in Norway. Tea from China or Ceylon, take your choice; and next week you can go there and choose your turkey or goose for your Christmas dinner.

Mr. Arthur Clowes manages a very brisk busi- ness in Iforsemarket-street. For Christmas he has got a good display of tempting eatables. What with English pork, home-potted meats, home-cured hams (doesn't that sound homely and nice?), plum puddings, delicious little mince pies, ana so cheap, too! tinned goods, packets of seedless raisins, sauces, chutnies (both mango and fruit), real at cakes and shortbread from Scotland, one scarcely knows to what delicacy to rush to first.
Messrs. Ben Few and Son are grocers, confec- tioners and butchers, a rare combination for Christmas trade, of which full advantage has been taken.

When you have satisfied your epicurean taste and done buying dainties for your Christmas festive board, and you return to the round of every-day edibles, Messrs. J. Povey and Son can supply you with them. Ile keeps splendid bacon for cold January mornings; a variety of cheeses for supper, and biscuits, butter, tea, cur- rants, raisins, tinned meats and every other eatable in the ordinary grocery line at reason- able prices.

gracious assemblage of countenances airoisni you at this truly festive season you ouiit at k&.O to be happy, and if you are happy yourself you will diffuse happiness around you. A kind heart is a fountain of gladness, it makes everything in its vicinity freshen into smiles, and a joyous disposition is always contagious. Verily it is a great thing to have one day in the year at least, when you are suroltif a welcome wherever you go, and of having, so to speak, the world all thrown open to you. These Christmas dinners, how cheery they are! What a great effect they have in making us fond of our homes, and they make the times merrier, kinder and better.. I can truly say with one of our old poets: " I like them well—the curious preciseness 7.And all-pretended gravity of those That seek to banish hence these harmless sports Have thrust away much ancient honesty.',!, However; I hope you will all have once more a real, downright jovial Christmas, and I wish you a very good appetite.to enjoy your Christmas dinner. E. W.

div.head: pASSIJIG WEEK,
div.p: pASSIJIG WEEK,

OUR CHRISTMAS GREETING. 4 Here's a health to all those that we love, Here's a health to all those that love us' Here's a health to all those that love them that love those That love them that love those that love us.

THE COMING FESTIVAL. Everything seems to be in perfect order for the coming festival. Our first thoughts go out to those who may be afflicted in mind, body, or estate, and we wish them a happy termination' of their troubles. But for the great mass of our people-this will be one of the happiest Christ- mases on record, trade being good and the weather remaining open and allowing the lower paid class of labourer to put in `,` full time." To-morrow Is the shortest day, a 'fact which will be recognised with a sigh of relief and hopefulness by not a few people.

THE OUTDOOR POOR. At the eleventh hour the 'Warrington Guar- dians have altered their decision not to concede a little Christmas gratuity to their poor in receipt of outdoor relief, and theft latest deci- sion to grant is. 6d. to each adult and 9d. to each child extra during the festive week will commend itself to the ratepayers at the season of goodwill.. Why the Guardians should want to depart from the usual custom of every Board in England cannot be fathomed. The cost of :the .gratuity will be.about £2O, a mere drop in the bucket-or g'old they propose to spend upon -new:and.palatial offices, and not a fraction of a half-penny in the .pound. Surely to squabble over a £2O note is false economy. The con- cession was not granted without a grudge, and it was only carried on the casting vote or the Chairman. Yet this money given 'SO stintingly will be the most apiveciated gift of the season by the recipients.

div.head: SOUTH LAI4ARK ELECTION RESULT.
div.p: SOUTH LAI4ARK ELECTION RESULT.

Last week-end the election agents had a sharp passage-at-arms over the South Lanark election result. That election was a , three-cornered fight, in which the Conservative candidate scrambled in by 251 votes, the. Labour man having attracted no fewer than 1,674 supporters, mainly, it may be assumed, taken directly from the Liberal- ranks. As a matter of . fact, both the Liberal and the Lebow candidates advocated Home Rule. The Liberal placard announcing the result locally was first on the walls and claimed that the result was a victory for Home Rule by 1,423. This claim appears to have staggered the opposition camp, whose bill, when it appeared, put the Labour vote and the Conservative vote • together, and claimed the result as a heavy... majority "against the Government.". It alsp- announced that South Lanark stood by the "Union Jack." In view of the actual policies advocated during the con- test, it certainly looked as though S Lanark Unionists had slipped off the first r of the Tory programme, Tariff Reform, and badly fractured its head on the second plank, Home Rule: The wonder is they had sufficient courage to claim it as a "victory." In one sense it was a very fitting victory—a minority victory in a minority :cause:. .

But that by the way. In this game okwit the Liberals had the next call, but they did not avail themselves of the right: The Conserva- tives, however, were not quite easy, so they played again and-posted a placard saying that everybody was "laughing at it---which was quite lrue. Everybody Is still. laughing, though, in, Sankey-street their laugh, like .their humour; is said tO be oh' the-sad side.

div.head: COMMITTEE FRICTION
div.p: THE COMMITTEE FRICTION

The .friction which has arisen between the Education Committee and the Health Com- mittee, over the appointment of a school nurse furnishes an unedifying spectacle which ought to be\ studiously avoided in the future. The Health Committee claim as their prerogative the right to appoint all officials connected with health, while the Education Committee contend that as the nurse is a direct employe of their body they are the proper authority to make the appointment. In the course of the discussion at the Education Committee it was said Sir George Newnian, a Board of Education official, stated that Warrington was the only town in

England where the Health Committee are allowed; to make this class of appointment. Now the matter will be thrashed out with the General, Purposes Committee, otherwise the Council, sitting in private, as arbitrators, it is to be hoped a modus operandi will be reached whereby such unnecessary wrangling will be obviated.

div.head: SCHOOL EXEMPTIONS.
div.p: SCHOOL EXEMPTIONS.

The granting of wholesale. exemptions to children to leave school below the proper 'age for leaving is a raise point with,some members of the Wallington Education Committee.. At one afternoon session 116 exemptions were granted by the School Attendance Sub-com- mittee, and, as Mr. J. Upson stated, this large total could not have been thoroughly investi- gated. There is too much of the wholesale about the number of the cases to be dealt with in the detail required by the Act. That there are truly necessitous cases no one can disppte, but a careful -winnowing -process -must be fol- )(mod so that-the genuine -grain may be sifted from the chaff. This can -never be done when the sub-Committee take on the "rush" job of coping with 119 cases in one brief afternoon. Mr. Upson showed that one of the cases in the 116 exempted out of the 119 applications was not one of necessity, and there are doubtless more of the same kind. It has also been stated that trade unionists—other than the leaders— favour these exemptions. This is inaccurate, for two reasons. Trade unionists desire their children .to be as highly educated as the children of any other class; if riot, why does the Ruskin College at Oxford and: the Labour College at London exist? They are also against child labour in every form, while the sub-com- mittee, in granting the exemptions, are flooding the market with cheap child labour..

div.head: CHARMING WIDOW.
div.p: THE CHARMING WIDOW.

JACK REMINGTON. She is modest, but not bashful; Free and easy, but not bold; Like an apple, ripe and mellow; Not too young, and not too old; Half-inviting, half-repulsing, Now advancing, and now shy; There is mischief in her dimple; There is danger in her eye.

She has studied human nature; She is schooled in all her arts; She has taken her diploma As the mistress of all hearts, She can tell the very MOMOnt When to sigh and when to smile, 0, a maid is sometimes charming, But the widow all the while!

Are you sad? How very serious Will her handsome face become? Are you angry? She is wretched, Lonely, friendless, tearful, dumb. Are you mirthful? How her laughter, Silver sounding, will ring out. She can lure and catch and play you As the angler does the trout.

You old bachelors of forty, Who have grown so bold and wise; Young Americans of twenty, With the love look in your eyes, You may practice all your lesqons Taught by Cupid since the fall; Rut I know a charming widow, Who can win and fool you all.

div.p: A FIItST PLANK AND A. SLENDEI

div.head: TIE.
div.p: TIE.
The delegate who, at the Tariff Reform. League Conference at Manchester, moved a
resolution declaring Tariff Reform to be the
first plank of the . party programme, made a striking confession. Some of the delegates, he said, including himself, were onlf bound to the
Unionist party by a slender tie, and that tie was " the .first constructive policy." It would
appear, then, that the Unionist party, while clamouring for a General Election on the
alleged ground that the sense of the country is against the Home Rule Bill, and should be taken
on this single issue, is itself dependent for support from not only voters, but active workers who have no sympathy with its anti- Home Rule crusade, and only desire a General
Election to accelerate the establishment of a
Protective tariff. Mr. AUSTEN CHAMBERLAIN

professed himself an unrepentant believer in food taxes. All he repented was the unuisdom and inexpediency of the course pursued by the leaders of his party when they decided to post- pone the food tax issue till the, next. General Election but one. Never in his life, he ex-
claimed, had he been called upon to make so deep and bitter a sacrifice as when he passively acquiesced in the acceptance of the Edinburgh programme.
"Unionist first, Tariff Reformer afterwards"; such is Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S formula. It is_ a -.formula asserted in quite good faith.
Indeed, it is 4 very ingenuous- formula, for, being interpreted, it means that the Opposition are clinging to the hope that, by means of an
anti-liome.Rule crusade, they can win support for Tariff'-.RefcTin in quarters where it is
anathema. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, who says that he can hardly think of Tariff Reform because the
Irish question is so absorbing, disclaims an,
wish to hustle Mr. ASQUITH. At the same time

he declares that " the sands are running out" —an historical phrase with sinister associations —and profess to believe there may be a "spontaneous" conflagration in Ulster any day. " Spontaneous " is a good •word to use
where there has been so Much lighting up and fanning. But Tariff Reformers, through long- training, cannot help using terms and figures that represent an. idea quite the reverse of the
meaning that usually attaches to them.

div.head: MOST INJURIOUS TO UNIONIST
div.p: MOST INJURIOUS TO UNIONIST
PROSPECTS!

Poor Tariff Reform cannot know the differ- ence between its friends and its enemies. We are not referring :to the uncertainty caused by such leader-followers as Mr. BONAR LAW, who throws over food taxes, and. even then says his party may be kept out of office -for forty years. At the Conference at Manchester this week It- was resolved, on the initiative of the Stockport branch, to condemn the action of "so-called Unionist papers in attempting to create /an unfavourable opinion tovietds Tariff Reform by publishing articles and letters attacking that policy, and by cutting down or altogether ex- cluding items of news and letters calculated to assist the first constructive policy of the party, as recently re-affirmed by. the Unionist leaders." It is evidently intended to be a cruel cut to call these papers that are coming to their senses, " so-called." "So-called," indeed! But what of such newspapers as "The Yorkshire Post," the greatest Conservative organ outside Lon- don? In a recent issue of that influential North- country paper publicity was grudgingly_given to a letter. front Mr. Jons FAIRFAX, a Manchester Tariff Refornier.- In a footnote to the letter in cillestion the Editor-says :

We print Mr. Fairfax's letter, but as we are strongly of opinion that a discussion of any Tariff Reform principles and proposals would cause most serious injury to the pros- pects of the Conservative and Unionist party, not only in Yorkshire and Lancashire, but over the whole of the North of England, we shall not publish any further correspondence on this subject."

This is a cruel cut of .another kind. Fancy a party being told frankly that a discussion of its " first constructive policy" would do Most serious 'injury to its own prospeals. Of course, "The Yorkshire Post" is perfectly honest. The paper limits the prOspect-blight- ing properties of this most colossal humbug in modern politics to the North of England, and especially Lancashire and YbrkShire. , The so-called policy may do for the sleepy South, though we expect to see many newspapers with farming areas to cover following in the wake of "The Yorkshire Post." Now that taxes on food are forsaken, farmers will begin to look to their " prospect " ; and they will not see the force of the argument if they are told they must pay more for their machinery while the price of corn is not similarly manipulated. The " prospect "is becoming hazy all round. Forty , years did the Tariff champion say? Forty years?

"The' Yorkshire Post" reluctantly gave its support to the Tariff Reform programme. It is one of the first to throw that programme over. Last in, first out. As things go, since Tariff Reform blurred the morals of the British Press, this is quite an honourable record.

div.head: PEACE REFUSED.
div.p: PEACE REFUSED.
Cheshire Line, s Committee Reject
Offer of the Platelayers.
LIFE ON £1 Os. 6d. PER WEEK.

There was a development last night in con- nection with the platelayers' strike at Warring- ton which went to indicate the stubborn attitude assumed by the Cheshire Lines Committee. The men offered to accept conciliation and sub- mit their case to an independent arbitrator, but the manager wrote yesterday: "The com- mittee cannot agree to re-open the present con- ciliation agreement." This means that a gad- lock has now occurred, but it is significant to those who know the terms of the conciliation agreement. Under that the committee are not empowered to increase the hours of labour or to decrease the pay, but nothing is said about giving 'increases, and had this matter gone to an arbitrator there seems little doubt but he would recommend an increase in wages. Evi- dently the Cheshire Lines Committee have noted this fact, and hence their refusal to nego- tiate for a settlement.

div.head: Men Determined.
div.p: Men Determined.

The Warrington platelayers on strike are set- ting an example of determination and solidarity which is having a marked effect on the men elsewhere on the Cheshire Lines. They have issued, an appeal to local trade unionists to con- tribute to the strike fund, and to this there should be a ready response, as the strikers are not only fighting a battle for themselves, but for the "bottom doge" elsewhere. In this appeal, which is headed "Life on .21 Os. 6d. Per week cannot be tolerated," the men state: " We have hard work to obtain the bare necessaries; luxuries are out of the question; and some of us have not a change of clothes. Our work is fairly bard, and the wages harder still. Our wtves and children wafer without reasonable cause, because we are merely beasts of burdeu,% doomed to a life• of drudgery by our circum- stances."

• Worse Than Ten Years Ago. • 'At-a meeting of the Vigilance Committee held in Warrington on Thursday evening, Mr. J. C- Edwards, in the course of a pointed speech, placed the men's case plainly before the public. He declared that not only were the conditions of the men worse, but that the wages of the men were worse than they were ten years ago, in ,face of the assurance given by good authorities that the value of the sovereign had been re- duced to 14s. 2d. It was also stated that this agitation really had its origin on the hearth- stones of their homes, for their wives had con- vinced them that they could no l- -ger make ends meet on the miserable wages i ' e workers received; and that before coming ont on strike they had exhausted all the means at their dis- posal to bring about a peacefill settlement.

Labour Exchange " Blaekkgs." It was stated that in Manchester a number of " blacklegs" from the Labour Exchange had been stopped by the pickets on the way to the lines, but had turned back upon the position being explained to them. Commenting upon this, one speaker said that if use of this kind was to be made of the Labour Exchanges to the detriment of the interests of trade unionists when they were fighting for better conditions, efforts should be made to have the Exchanges removed. Resolutions were adopted thanking other grades for their assistance, appealing for public financial help to be sent to Mr. G. Marsh, Railway Cottage, Cathshead, and warning all permanent way men to depend entirely on their own officials for information in connection with the dispute.

div.head: DEATH OF A LOCAL J.P.
div.p: DEATH OF A LOCAL J.P.
Mr. W. Richardson Dies Siddenly

Mr. William Richardson, J.P., a well-known Warringtonian, died somewhat suddenly at his residence, "Holly Bank," Walton, on Wednes- day morning. He was 65 years of' age, and although he had been, in indifferent health for some time, he was only taken seriously ill on Monday. On Sunday morning he was perform- ing warden's duties at St. Thomas' Church, Stockton Heath, with which he was actively connected. A very active business man, he had for many years been a partner with his brother in the firm of Messrs. W. and J. Richardson• coal dealers, Warrington. He was a director of the Longford Wire Company and a trustee of the Warrington Savings Bank and chairman of one of the important sub-committees of the bank. In 1904 he was made a justice of the peace. In addition to being a member of the Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club, he ives an enthusiastic member of the Warrington Golf Club and was the joint holder of the Academy Cup. He was a Conservative in poll- tics. He leavesa widow and two sons. Mr. W. Richardson, his son, is captain of the local cricket club:

- At the Borough Court on Wednesday, the Chairman, Mr. J. WNHayward, said that as a magistrate Mr. Richardson attended with fre- quency and consistency to his duties, and had given valuable service as a licensing megig" trate. They had lost an able, courteous and .steady magistrate.

Mr. C. Jackson Holmes endorsed what the Chairman had said. Mr. Richardson had ren- dered valuable serviee to the Savings Bank. He performed all his duties with a thorough- ness that it would be impossible to excel. Alderman Smethurst said he had always found Mr. Richardson an upright, just and straig ward gentleman. htfor-

div.head: LOCAL INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: LOCAL INTELLIGENCE.
Alderman Pierpoint's Condition.
Dr. Law reports thaf Alderman Pierpoint con- tinues to make satisfactory progress at the Warrington Infirmary.
Change at the Workhouse.
Mr. T. P. Eccleston, late superintendent clerk at Padgate Cottage Homes and now at Manches- ter, has been appointed Assistant Workhouse Master, in place of Mr. 0. A. Moss, who has resigned. ,
The Scarlet Fever.
Seven cases of scarlet fever were reported last week. The cases in hospital now number 53.
Councillor Birtles' Condition.
, We were informed last night that there is no Change in the condition of Councillor Birtles, who is seriously ill.
Births and Deaths.
There were 44 births last week, 17 males and 27 females, giving a rate of 32.3. There were 26 deaths, 11 males and 15 females giving a rate ef 18.2.

div.head: Motor Accident.
div.p: Motor Accident.

Delia Knight (7), 17, Plumpton-street, who was knocked down by a. motor car on Saturday evening and received concussion of the brain, was reported last night to be progressing satis- factorily at the Infirmary. The- child ran off the footpath at Bank Quay Bridge and was knocked down by a cat belonging to Mr. Henry Forster Harrison, 288, Lytham-road, Blackpool. She was conveyed in the car to the Infirmary.

div.head: Smoke Tit for Tat.
div.p: Smoke Tit for Tat.

The Town Council recently complained to the Warrington guardians about the black smoke 'emitted from the Workhouse. At the Guardians' meeting on Wednesday they decided to have a bit of their own back. It was reported that a great nuisance was occasioned at the Workhouse by the emission of .dense -black smoke from the Fever Hospital, controlled by the Council. The Clerk was instructed to write the Town Clerk a complaint about the nuisance.

School Grants in Danger. - Unless new schools are quickly provided :the Warrington Education Committee are in danger of losing a considerable portion of the grants from the Board Of Education. Mr. E. Plinston reported this fact to the Education Committee on Monday, and hoppd the Sites and Buildings Committee would hurry on the erection of the new schools. Councillor Pemberton said archi- tects were appointed in June, 1912, for the Oak- wood-avenue School, and he wanted to know why the specifications had not yet been got out. This meant another six months' delay." The dis- cussion was ruled out of order.

div.head: Ebenezer Band of Hope.
div.p: Ebenezer Band of Hope.

A Band of. Hope entertainment was held in the Ebenezer Church, Buttermarket-street,, on Mon- day evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. 11. Thornton. A temperance address was given by Mr. H. Wright, in which were given instances of the evil of alcohol. Recitations were pro- vided by Edith Ridgway, Emily Higham, Edith Hinchcliffe, and Miss Lily Hibbert. Action Songs were rendered by .the children. A Solo was also sung by Mrs. Bebbington. 414. glee song, entitled "The village church," was .given by members of the Band of Hope. A dialogue, " Grandad's supper beer," was given by Beatrice Houghton, Thomas Pox and George Hasler, and a dialogue, "The neighbours next door," was performed by the Misses Sarah Fox, Sarah Dodds, Lily llibbert, Annie Bibby and Jane Birchall, and Messrs. Harry Richardson and John Barlow.

Buckley-street Band of Hope. The Band of Hope- entertainment at Buckley- street on Monday evening was provided by the Warrington Band of Hope Union Juvenile Choir under the direction of Mr. A. Spruce, who ren- dered the various items in a creditable manner. The programme included: Part-songs by the tchoir, "0 the summer" (Coleridge Taylor), "The voyage" (Evans), "Jack and Jill" (Jarvis); songs by Ada Hamer, "Father, don't, stay away late," and "Poor child of a drunkard"; song by Lily Pye, "Curley Head"; also recitation, "The abstainer's alphabet"; song by Hilda Taylor; "Granny's reason," and also the; reci= ta.tion, "Marching orders"; duet by Ada Hamer and Evelyn Naylor, "bright summer" .(Vin- cent); recitation .by Hilda Hewitt, "The Eng- lishman," and a recitation by G. Watkins, "Mpg Merrilees." Miss Spruce was the accompanist. Mr. J. W. Bradley presided and also gave a con- vincing addressen the evils of strong drink. At the close a number of pledges Were taken.

div.head: Guardians' New Offices.
div.p: The Guardians' New Offices.

The question of the site for the new offices for the Warrington Guardians was, again cdis- cussed at a meeting on Wednesday. The Sites Committee reported a conference with the Mayor over a site near, the Town Hall in Sankey-street, but recommended that the work be proceeded with on another site at Winmarleigh-street.— Mr. A. J. Jolley moved that. the ,matter 'be de- layed until February to give the Council a chance to submit definite proposals.—The Rev. A. M. Mitchell seconded, and thought all Public offices should be concentrated in one black. Miss Broadbent said it would ben pity to pull down the beautiful old houses in Sankey-street. —Mr. Bent, the chairman, said the Sankey-street site would be double the price of the site they had in view. The council would erect costly buildings, and the Guardians would have to erect the same costly structure.—Mr. Garnett asked if the Guardians could not secure the . Labour Exchange Buildings, seeing that the Labour Exchange was to be removed into a new building.—The Chairman : That is for the cora, mittee.—The Board decided not to delay the matter until February.

div.head: Junior Liberals and Public Duty.
div.p: Junior Liberals and Public Duty.

4The annual meeting and election of officers was held at the rooms 'in HOrsemarketzritreet on Monday evening. Unfortunately Mr. E. Lloyd Jones was unable to occupy the chair, owing to indisposition. Mr. B. G. Hughes pre- sided. Mr. E. Wallington, the secretary, briefly submitted a report of work done during the past year, and touched upon the lectures, open-air campaign, garden fete and sale of work, all of which were pronounced successes. At no far distalit 'date the people of Warrington would see the Junior Liberals undertaking prominent work in connection with the borough, and thus bringing honour to the association to which they belonged. Mr. L. F. Hughes, treasurer, sub- mitted his financial report, and both • were adopted.. The officers were elected as follows: President, Mr., A. H. Crosfield ; chairman, Mr. E. Lloyd Jones; deputy chairman, Mr. G. Toul- min; secretary, Mr. E. Wallington; assistant secretary, Mr. E. Lloyd Jones; treasurer, Mr, L. F. Hughes; committee, Messrs. J. H. Booth, 11.. B. Bradburn, P.ll. Brown, A. Cox, ES. Chil- ton, J. Ford, J. Griffiths, J; A. Houghton, E. G. Hughes, J. L. Jones, J. H. Owen, H. Slater, W. H. Sanders, E. A. Sanders, N. Wilkinson, B. Williams and W. E. Wright.

Brutality of Boxinty. "The Brutality of Boxing—Engltsb...._and French," was the subject of the Rev. 11. Ogden's sermon at Golborne-street Baptist Church on Sunday evening. The recent boxing, .fiasco at the National Sporting Club was brutal, low and coarse. A writer had suggested that there wait not the slightest excuse for the knock- out blow, tnd he described the position of the tall Englishman lying writhing in agony upon the ground. One was, compelled to see; that that was an exhibition of strength that brought, no glory.to God. What amazed any reader of the event must be to learn the fabnlou!i4 prices that were, 'paid to see .the fight; how the wealthy of London crowded to see the exhibition, and one felt that if such men would pay those • linge prices to see such an exhibition, the spirit of hooliganism was not confined to the slums and street corners. The exhibition was a national degradation of the abuse of the glorious gifj; that God had given to young men.

div.head: Boy Scouts Make Merry.
div.p: Boy Scouts Make Merry.
'KITCHEN RANGES, FIRE GRATES, TlLES.—Large ,atock, reasonable prices.—J. S. GARLAND, Iron- Monger, 61 to 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.

" Crosfield's Own" Boy Scouts made merry on Thursday night, when they held their annual hotpot supper in the. men's -dining hall. Their guests included their Scout Commissioner (Col. Thomas), Capt. Appleton, Mr. Starkey, and other welt-known gentlemen. Following the supper Colonel Thomas distributed prizes to members of the troop. This was succeeded by ,exhibitions of physical culture, ambulance work, quarterstaff (contests, fire drill and box- ing, whilst the buglers, in command of Bugler- Instructor Bowker, gave numerous "calls." Scoutmaster Seymour, Jones was in command. An excellent Iconcert was given, at which the following were the artistes Mr. Brobbin, Mr. J. Newns, Leader Boyle and Scouts llothwell and Pepperall. The followin'g were the prize- winners: Best patrol leader, Patrol Leader J. Earle; best all-round Scout, Scout Peacock; best ambulance man, Leader Yearsley ;:' best signal- ler, Scout Pacey; best cook, Scout Hough; smartest Scout on parade, Drummer Burns; next smartest Scout on parade, Drummer Smith.

div.head: Gift of Needlework.
div.p: Gift of Needlework.
The Rev. Hugh Williamson, of the Bold- street Wesleyan Church, desires to acknowledge the receipt of a parcel of clothing from the Warrington Needlework Guild.

div.head: Honour for Dr. Manson.
div.p: Honour for Dr. Manson.

The degree of M.D. was conferred on Dr. Manson, of Warrington, by Edinburgh Univer- sity at "Degree Day," on Wednesday. This is the highest medical qualification the great Scottish Medical School can bestow.

div.head: Bench and Bar's Greetings.
div.p: Bench and Bar's Greetings.

The season's greetings were exchanged at the County Court on Thursday, when Mr. A. Browne, on behalf of the legal profession, wished his Honour Judge Stanger the compliments of the season, and a happy and proVerous New Year. His Honour returned the good wishes.

div.head: Essay from the Pictures.
div.p: Essay from the Pictures.

The result Of the " Queen " es-say competition is as follows: 1, A. Worthington ~Orford school; 2, R. Gibson, Beamont Council-School; 3, E. Sankey, Sacred Heart School; special consola- tion prize, A. E. Spence, Secondary School. It is pleasing to note that over 200 essays were sent into the competition, and, judging .from the reading of same, it is quite evident that the children have taken a great interest in the life and reign of Victoria the Good.

div.head: Church Lads' Whit Drive.
div.p: Church Lads' Whit Drive.

The members of the, Warrington Church Lad? Brigade -N.C.O.'s Mess held a whist drive on Tuesday night in the Mess Room at Colonel Appleton's office. The M.C. was Lieutenant Bottomley, and 'the winners were Sergeant- Bugler H. Goodwin, Quartermaster-Sergeant Astall, Corporal Rutter, Corporal Dobson, Cor- poral Ashton, and Staff-Sergeant Rooke. The Adjutant, Captain Sankey, and Lieutenant Johnson were present.

div.head: Warrington P.S.A. Open Meeting.
div.p: Warrington P.S.A. Open Meeting.

A successful open meeting of the Warrington P.S.A. was held on Sunday afternoon. Mr. 'J. B. Starkey presided, and gave an address on "Usefulness." • The Rev: H. Ogden was the chief speaker, and he gave an inspiring address on '-" The two prophets The lesson was read by Mr. Minshall. Mr. nigginsim and Mr. R. Nelson also took part in the service. "The Star of Bethlehem" was excelleiftly given as a cornet solo by Mr. W. Rutter, and the band, under the conductorship of Mr. J. E. Hannan, admirably dispersed selections:

"The Boy Would Be a Sailor." Gordon Stanley Hawley Newall, of Drachen- fels, Lower Walton, a scholar of the Municipal Secondary School for the past three and a half years, has been placed 43rd on the list in the examination for candidates for entry as boy artificers into H.M. Navy, and will proceed to Devonport to join his ship in January next. Gordon S. H. Newall .was recommended by the Education Committee, on the result of an exam- ination, locally conducted, to compete with boys recommended by certain other ducation Anthorities in the country, and is the second Warrington boy to secure -entry into the Navy as boy artificer by -this means.

div.head: Surprise Gift to Church Worker.
div.p: Surprise Gift to Church Worker.

An interesting event took place in the Insti- tute Room a the young men at Golborne-street Baptist Church. At the close of the annual business meeting of the Institute a presentation was made to Mr. T. Davis the treasurer of the Institute. Mr. Dayis, who, in addition to being treasurer for the young men, is captain of the Boys' Brigade, has stood by the Institute in times of great stress. The gift of a silver- mounted umbrella came as a great surprise to the recipient. The Chairman, the Rev. H. Ogden, made the presentation in suitable terms, which Mr. Davis acknowledged With much feeling. He was delighted \ with the gift, not for its value, but because of the goodwill which it expressed. The gift enshrined that goodwill which he much appreciated.

div.head: Education and Citizenship.
div.p: Education and Citizenship.

On Wednesday evening, at the Old Academy, Mr. Norman Nield opened a discussion on the question, `` Is modern English education con- ducive to good citizenship?" He maintained that good citizenship demanded a full expres- sion of the old axiom "noblesse oblige," the fulfilment of which seemed almost an unknown quantity in our social life to-day. The Educa- tion Act of 1870 was never intended to give education in its higher sense, but was simply meant to provide instruction which would raise the industrial unit value, just as a farmer gave spent grain to his cows to increase the yield of milk. Messrs. E. G. Burgess, H. H. Taylor, D. J. Dunn, C. S. Woods and T. E. Knowles also took part in the discussion.

div.head: Visit of a Famous Band.
div.p: Visit of a Famous Band.

The magnificent band of the 2nd Battalion ' South Lancashire Regiment will pay a visit of a fortnight's duration to Warrington and the neighbourhood next month. The concerts given by this band seven years ago, when it came to Warrington at the time of the unveiling of the Regimental Memorial to those of the regiment who fell in the South African War, will be within the memory of most Warringtonians, and the splendid reception given to them on that occasion is still remembered in the regiment The band will arrive at Warrington on January 3rd, and on the evening of Sunday, the 4th, will give its opening concert at the Hippodrome at 8.15 p.m., being assisted by several well-known local artistes, who have kindly given their ser- vices. The building has been most kindly placed at the disposal of the band free, and the entire proceeds of this concert will be given to the funds of the Warrington Infirmary.

Baptist "Rally." . The committeg of the Lancashire and Cheshire Association of -Baptist Churches met at Gol- borne-street Baptist Church on Thursday for the transaction of annual business. Luncheon and tea were served by friends of the Golborne- street church. In the evening a " rally " was held. Mr. A. Watson, Rochdale, moderator of county churches, presided, and expressed a de- sire to see all the churches in the counties in- side the association. Many at present, espe- cially in rural parts, were leading a lonely life, and worked in isolation. A united life was im- perative in everything to-day, and unity was needed, not only unity amongst Baptists, but unity amongst all the churches.—The Rev. W. Owen, Manchester, expressed pleasure at having been able to visit Warrington for the fourth time this year. When they surveyed God's work they discovered that the prosperity of one was the prosperity of all, and the success of the Baptist Church reflected upon the churches of the whole kingdom. He was greatly pleased .with what had been accomplished at Golborne- street, and whatever prosperity prevailed there would be felt throughout the whole country.-- The Rev. H. Ogden stated that he had received a telegram from the Rev. J. F, Shearer, Liver- pool, qcpressing regret at not being able to attend. Two anthems were admirably rendered by the choir under •the leadership of Mr. Barnes.
Our Almanac. We present with this issue our Almanac for 1914. A copy is given with each "-Examiner."

div.head: Help for Dublin Strikers.
div.p: Help for Dublin Strikers.
The -Warrington Trades Council have for- warded X 43 towards the sufferers through the prolonged strike in Dublin.
Mr. Frederick Taylor.
Mr. Taylor, Green Bank, Manchester-road, has been confined to his bed for some weeks. and last night his condition was critical.
Next Week.
Next week the -Christmas number a " The Examiner" will contain much seasonable read- ing, including special stories written by well- known writers.

div.head: Forthcoming Balls.
div.p: Forthcoming Balls.

The annual children's ball in connection with the Infirmary takes place in the Parr 1-101 on New Year's Eve, December 30th. The- Mayor And Mayoress will .receive the guests. The Warrington Catholic Charity Ball takes place in the same hall on 20th January.

div.head: Junior Conservative Hall.
div.p: Junior Conservative Hall.

The new Junior Conservative Hall to be used as a club by members of the Warrington Junior Conservative Association Was opened on Thurs- day evening by Sir Gilbert Greenall. Mr. H. Parr,. the president; Presided ovei a large Attendance. An address, chiefly. on.. the Home Wile question, was delivered by Mr. Brian 'O'Donnell. A vote of thanks to Sir Gilbert -Oreenall• was 'proposed by Mr. Hall, seconded by Mr. W. P. Hylands, and supported by Mr. 'O'Donnell. • •

div.head: Tax on Corn Again.
div.p: The Tax on Corn Again.

'Alderman Bennett, .at a Manchester Confer- *nee on Tariff Reform, on Monday. moved : "That this conference, though not opposed isto any well-considered policy which is calculated tu. promote the interests of agriculture, is of .-opinion that the most effective solution is to be -found in the adoption of the full programme of 'Tariff Reform, Which would raise the level Of -wages, restore the welfare of 'our greatest in- dustry, assist the Colonies, and lead to true Imperial uniol.'-7 Having been seconded by ,Mr. Dunn, Warrington, the resolution was 'cairied unanimously.

div.head: Free Church Boys' Brigade.
div.p: Free Church Boys' Brigade.

The quarterly church parade took place at Latchford Baptist Chapel on Sunday. The battalion mustered in the strength of 1.20 officers and boys at Victoria ,Park; and Marched to the vhaml.,—behind the Massed bugle bands. The Rev. J. S. Chedburn, chairman of the Battalion 'Council, presided, and Councillor R. Ilenshall •delivered a stirring address on the experiences .of Shadrach,:. Meshach and Abed-nego. After the service Councillor llenshall inspected the !battalion and spoke in the highest terms- of the appearance and conduct of the lads; wishing 'the movement every success.

div.head: Fell in the Locks.
div.p: Fell in the Locks.

Mr. Ridgway conducted an inquest in the Parish Room, Grappenhall, yesterday after- noon, on Richard Livingstone (27), 344, Thel- Grappenhall, who was drowned in the canal at Walton Locks on Wednesday.even- ing. Deceased, who was a foreman employed by Messrs. R. A..2•Taylor, Ltd., was crossing the locks between 6 and,7 p.m., when in the Ark- ness he fell into the water. The splash and shout were heard, and grappling operations took place, with the result that the body was re- covered early the next morning. The jury re- turned a verdict of "Accidentally_ drowned," and expressed Sympathy -with - the deceased's mother.

div.head: Coroner's Practical Sympathy-.
div.p: Coroner's Practical Sympathy-.

A pitiable story was revealed at the Coroner's Court on Wednesday, when Coroner Brighouse inquired into the death of Margaret Hannah Jowett (3), of 11, Williamson's-square. So sad was the. story that Mr. Brighouse allowed • the parents £2 out of the poor box.----Elizabeth Ann Jowett, the mother, said while she was attend- ing to a baby upstairs the deceased went into the house and caught fire. The screams of the little one hurried the 'mother to the spot and she found the child standing at the 'door with her clothes on • fire. A man wrapped his ('oat' round the child and extinguished the flames. She was removed to the Infirmary, where she died on . Saturday. The 'child was wearing flannelette underclothing at the time of the accident. A verdict of "Accidental death" wag returned.

div.head: Night Photography.
div.p: Night Photography.

A lecture that will long he remembered by the 40 members of .the Warrington Photographic Society was given on Tuesday by Mr. William- son, of Cockermouth. A remarkable series of lantern pictures illustrated each point, and these included the widest range of night sub- jects, from brilliant scenes in the heart of London and New York, or the White City, Man- chester, down to the most dimly-lighted back street, illuminated by a single gas lamp. The details in the shadows of all his pictures aston- ished the audience., especially where ordinary sitting-rboms were shown. And no wonder, when, Mr. Williamson exposes a plate for an hour, and then spends from one to two hours in its mani- pulation in the developer. How the plate keeps clear of fog was explained to. be due to abso- lutely pure water and chemicals, and keeping the solutions very cool.

div.head: Teachers and Children's Ball.
div.p: Teachers and Children's Ball.

At the December meeting of the Warrington 7rea,chers' Association, held in the Wycliffe Memorial Hall, ' a communicatiFn from the Mayor was read, in which he invited the co- ,operation of the teachers in making arrange- ments for a children's fancy dress ,bail, which is to be held in the Parr Hall on the evening of 'Thursday, January 15th, 1914. It was unani- mously resolved that the members do their 'utmost to make the function a SUCCOSs. A great amount of business for the forthcoming con- ference at Lowestoft was transacted. It was ,decided to support the following in their candi- dature for the National Executive: Miss Wood, Miss Conway, and Messrs. Alleott, Pearson and 'Sharpies. Messrs. J. Upson, W. H. Stansfield, .3. Cann, F. H. Longshaw, A. Malcolm, G. New- burn and Mrs. Stansfield were delegated to represent the local association. The Secretary, Mr. Longshaw, announced that the Membership had increased by 57 -during the year; he was -heartily 'congratulated on the success of his efforts.

'Mayor's " Royal " Welcome in Wales. At Fairbourne on Tuesday night the 'Mayor -of Warrington, ouncillor Peacock, presided --over a large and enthusiastic audience, who had 'come to the Pavilion to listen to various com- 'petitions, in. the Eisteddfod. This being his Irst appearance at Pairbourne since 'Mr. Pea- cock's election to the chair of chief magistrate .0f Warrington, great interest was taken in the *vent. A spontaneous and enthusiastic reception :Was given to the Mayor and Mayoress, as they - motored in earlier in the day. The school .children lined the route, waving flags, and a lmuquet of, flowers was presented to the Mayoress by the inhabitants. . The road and 'houses were decorated with 'bunting. In the -course of a short address Mr. Peacock said he. -was proud of being the recipient of the highest -honour which his native -town of Warrington -could give him, a position he never imagined would .so soon be conferred when elected a coun- cillor a short time previously. He at the same time regretted that the responsible duties of his high office would prevent him spending as much time at. Fairbourne as be had.intended. How- ever. there was some compensation in the fact that he considered the Tion.our given to him was • incidentally done to Fairhourne with which 'Place lie was now ,so intimately connected. On -Wednesday. at a dfoner giYcii by the Fairhoitrne *state to tiie in:habitants. the Mayor was presented with an address of congratulation and au autograph album from the residents.

div.head: Christmas Social.
div.p: Christmas Social.

The closing meeting of the Christmas Session of the Wycliffe Church Y.P.S.; held on Tuesday evening, was devoted to a social. Various games were indulged in by the large number present, and, Several members gave items of entertain- ment.

div.head: High Legh Sensation.
div.p: The High Legh Sensation.

Josepli Skitt, the ex-gamekeeper, of Hollowell- brow, High Legh, who met with sensational, injuries, as exclusively announced in "The Examiner" last week, through a trap gun ex- ploding while he was going through a wood be- tween High Legh and KnutsfOrd, was reported to be making favourable progress at Warring- ton Infirmary last night. His condition is, however, still 'serious.

div.head: Preachers for To-morrow.
div.p: Preachers for To-morrow.
Bewsey-road Wesleyan—Morning, Rev. W. A. Beckett; evening, Rev. E. Morgan; afternoon; " Messiah."
1-3 old-street Wesleyan—Morning, Rev. 11. iddlewood ; evening, 'Rev. IL Williamson— Portions of the "Messiah."
Cairo-street Chapel—Morning and evening, Dr. Mellor. .
Wycliffe Congregational—Morning and even- ing, Rev. T. T. James. " Messiah " at evening service.
Emmanuel Reformed Church Evening, Rev. T. Jaye. Latchford Baptist—Morning and evtking, Rev. J. S. Chedburn.
Golborne-street Baptist—Morning and even- ing Rev. 11. Ogden, Evening, " Messiah " selec- tions.
Christadelphians, Toft's Assembly Rooms, Bridge-street—Evening, Mr. J. 11. Gamble; Stockport.
Plays to Aid Lifeboat Fund.

It was an exceedingly happy night that was spent in the Latchford Parish Room on Thurs- day, when, by the efforts of a number of ama- teur performers, the Warrington branch of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution should benefit to the extent of about 1:20. Chief interest centred round the two playlets "The Peace- maker" and "Why Cupid came to Earl's Court." The former was a charmingly written comedy and the actors gLade the utmost of it: Mr. Montague Preston did the part of Dr. Bur- ton justice, as also did Miss Broadbent and Miss Adams in the roles of Elizabeth Lavender and Joyce Harford respectiv;ly, whilst as Richard Harford Mr: Withers was excellent. Miss M. Broadbent was excellent as Parsons, the ed ‘s W.iley Cupid came to Earl's Court"p‘rel ca evwaseYiu eineWhat, stronger in comedy than t production, and the audience en- joyed the excellent situations. The characters of Mr. Heary Robertson and his wife were capably sustained by Mr. W. B. Forshaw and Mrs. James Fairclough, whilst Mr. Brian Dick- son successfully adapted himself to an acct- able rendering of Harry Robertson. Miss Sylvia Broadbent as Phyllis did remarkably well, and as her friend, Beryl MacMurdo, Miss Adams again performed excellently. Mr. Clarke was very successful in interpreting the difficult role of Arthur Tilney, and Miss Broad- bent rather enhanced her reputation as an ama- teur actress by her rendition of Cookie. In addition to the playlets there were a number of songs, and these were well rendered by Miss Longdin and Mr. Eric Fairclough. Thp music was supplied by Mrs. Willett and her ladies' orchestra. Much praise for the success of the venture must be accorded Mrs. Broadbent, president of the local branch; Mrs. -Henry Greenall,, secretary; . and Miss G. Adams, organiser. -

THE HIPPODROME ATTRACTIONS. Pictures on Christmas Day.

Seats may now be booked for the Hippodrome on Christmas night, when two grand picture entertainments will be given at 6.15 and 8.15. Doors open 6 and 8. There will be an excellent programme of appropriate pictures at the usual prices. ' The ordinary programme of "star" vaude- ville turns for the five nights in the week,' in- eluding Boxing Day, will comprise: Alfred Woods and London Co in the morality play, "The Saint and the Sinner," which has had a _record of over 200 consecutive ,performances in London; The Five Jovers, gymnasts and acro- bats; C,larke, Sisters and Sterling, three maids at the piano; Jack Walsh, comedian; Ora, Zebra and Nara, acrobats, in "Pastimes on the Prairie"; Lawson and O'Dell, in comedy and harmony; and Albert Jenkins, the footballer comedian.

MARY STUART AT THEATRE ROYAL. This week's play has attracted large houses, and the company have added to their list of successes. On Christmas Day the picture, "Quo Vadis," will be shown, and should prove a good attrac- tion. On Boxing Day and the remainder of the week "Jane Shore," drama, will be pre- sented by the Stock Company, and on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, "For His Life" will be staged.
CHRISTMAS DAY AT THE PICTUREDROME. _

The picture palaces are to be opened oiLChrist- mas Day this year, and at the Pictu!lbdrome there will be two Performances on Christmas night, at 6.15 and 8.15. A special programme has been arranged for this occasion. On Boxing Day the , principal film 'will be "The Queen's Jewel," a magnificent dramatic master Piece, crammed with thrilling and sensational inci-
dents. On Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday next the chief picture at the Picturedrome will be " iounita," from gutter to footlights.
