A. number of pantomime favourites appear in the caste, and Miss Gladys Ilavius, who was the principal boy in pantomime at Dalin last year, and a Moss and Stoll favourite, will appear as Aladdin. Others stars" to appear will be 4t.=-4,4---117ft •

div.head: CHRISTMAS AT THE PARK PALACE
div.p: CHRISTMAS AT THE PARK PALACE

This popular place of entertainment and amusement will have special performances at 6.15 and 8.15 on Christmas night, when the principal film will be "Mary Stuart," an his- torical drama of extraordinary interest. This will also be the premier film for the remainder
of the week. For Monday, Tuesday and Wed- nesday. "A Man's Courage," an exciting pro- duction, will be shown.

div.head: NEW PICTURE HOUSE.
div.p: NEW PICTURE HOUSE.

The New Picture House also offets special attractions for Christmas Day, when the prin- cipal films will be: " Estretita," "The Call," Pimple, the Sport," "Love and Rubbish," and "Fortune Smiles," being the twelfth series of " What happened to Mary." There will be a continuous performance from 6.15. These pic- tures will be shown on Boxing Day and Satur- day.
• On Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday the principal picture will be "Four Dare Devils," a thrilling story of circus life; "An Old Man's Love Story," drama; and "Paris Zoo," comedy.

div.head: GREAT CIRCUS, LIVERPOOL.
div.p: THE GREAT CIRCUS, LIVERPOOL.

When Olympia, Liverpool, opens on Monday with the great circus, Jack Smiles—all smiles— will be there to keep the fun fast and furious. Jack Smiles has come back as fresh as ever with a clever new song, and with his inimitable dance. Smiles is a clever artiste, because he is alone at his own game, never copies—except he is doing the ever-mourned Leno's step at pre- sent—and "comes on" in an original get-up. Jack Smiles is following in his father's foot- steps, who had 45 years in the profession, with great •success. Yankee Boston and Young Ebony were the Dad and Jack in the old days, when they worked in " black "; later in "white" business they were known as the Two Bostons. Readers will recall the clever turn. They are talked about even to-day. It is only about three and, a half years ago since the father retired, and Young Ebony was re-introduced to the public as Jack Smiles. Working singly, he has made for himself a reputation.

div.head: MONEY GIVEN AWAY. T. Elder Hearn at the Hippodrome.
div.p: MONEY GIVEN AWAY. T. Elder Hearn at the Hippodrome.

T. Elder Hearn's visit to the hippodrome this week is the talk of the town. To many he has been a sort of a benevolent institution by giving away hundreds of postal orders to members of the audience. Mr. Hearn also causes roars of laughter as the lazy juggler and proves himself to be a most clever illusionist in "The Romance of a Studio." He plays several characters and changes with marvellous rapidity. He is one of the most versatile artistes we have seen for some time. Harry Moore tears the most artistic patters out of newspaper placards. Ernie Reah has a chatty style of tolling up-to-date yarns, and as the comedian at the piano he is decidedly a'success. Elton and Edwin give ragtime num- befi in a pleasing manner, and Alex. Lawson ifra success as the dancing equilibrist. " Will he do it?" is a comical film on the cinema,

div.head: DETECTIVE DRAMA. Royal Court Attraction.
div.p: DETECTIVE DRAMA. Royal Court Attraction.

"The Boy Detective" is a drama which can- not fail in its appeal to the popular parts of the house, for it bristles with exciting incidents, and the elucidating of the intricacies of the plot grips one from the outset. Mr. and Mrs. Harry Lyndon's Co. are drawing large houses to the Court Theatre, and each individual member adds his or her fair quota to the success of the play.

div.head: SCHOOL OF ART EXHIBITION.
div.p: SCHOOL OF ART EXHIBITION.
Clever Work Executed by Students.

IT—redounds to the credit of Warrington that we have in our midst such an excellent .centre for the developing of the love of art as that of the School of Art in Museum-street, and the exhibition now in progress of the students' work executed during the past year amply bears out this statement. The work covers a very wide range and is noticeable for itii-sincerity:— - The collections are arranged in two rooms and comprise oil and water-colours, from life and still life, sepia, light and shade, embroidery, studies from the antique, painters' and decora- tors' work, sign writing, tooled leather work, modelling, perforated metal work, &e. One of the most striking exhibitors is Mr. S. Clatworthy, whose light and shade drawings from life and from the antique are worthy of special attention. This student has done ex- ceedingly well, fdr, in addition to securing the County Council scholarship, tenable for three years, he has also obtained the new drawing certificate of the Board of Education. 114 was the only student from Warrington who entered for this certificate.

div.head: Fine Still Lite Pictures.
div.p: Fine Still Lite Pictures.

The paintings from still life are excellent and probably that of Miss Pearson, a water-colour, of a cottage window, is the choicest. The em- broidery art has made an appeal to several students, and their work is cleverly executed. Miss S. Clatworthy, Miss Pearson, Miss Shake- shaft and Miss Lowe contributing handsome specimens. Tooled leather work is a most interesting section, and perhaps here Miss Stewart is most prominent with fine work, whilst the illumin- ated vellum by Miss Shakeshaft is an admirable piece of work. The three specimens of modelling from the antique are particularly good and reflect credit upon Miss Clatworthy, Miss Acton and Mr. Essenhigh. The decorators' work is a strong section, and here Mr. De Prez seemed to have done the best. The wood-carving reflected credit on the students, as do the metal work and the perforated metal work. Altogether, the exhibition is a great success from the art point of view, and in some way tends to display the excellent training received in Warrington's School of Art.

div.head: PEOPLE'S COLLEGE CONCERT,
div.p: PEOPLE'S COLLEGE CONCERT,
A Notable Ahnual Event that Loses None of ts Attractiveness.
A PICTURE OF GLADNESS.

The Parr Hall was brimful of life and hap- piness on Thursday evening. On the plat- form the boys and girls of the People's College, to the number of 350, looked the picture of vitality and gladness. The audience crowded the hall in every part. Long experience has taught the people of Warrington that they may expect good fare on this 'annual night. The approach of Christmas with its general atmos- phere of festivity, and the infectious spirit of - hilarity which springs from the sight of chil- dren's faces and the sound of children's voices, conspire on such an occasion to make young again even people for whom the years pass quickly. No one could possibly feel old at a People's College concert. These concerts date back to the year 1871, and except for a period when no public hall was available, they have formed a regular feature of the life of the town. This was the sixteenth occasion on which the Parr Hall had been used for the event. Promptly at 7.30 the scholars took their places. Even the method of their arrival was a definite contribution to the enjoyment of the evening, and the long lines of daintily-dressed girls filing in from different entrances made n pretty scene, whilst on the upper part of the platform the boys added to the completeness of the picture. The long and well arranged pro- gramme was carried through from statt to finish with the greatest enthusiasm. It was a programme not merely interesting and enter- taining; these are mild terms for what indeed was a positive triumph. There was a vitality about the whole business which was stimulating to a degree. It is said of some concerts that they go with a swing; this went at a gallop and left everyone exhilarated at the end. ' The selections given by the whole school in chorus, of which there were many during the evening,' were all rendered effectively, and special praise must be awarded to the singing of • " Nirvana " and -"How we laugh," two items very different in conception, yet both inter- preted with great success. The soloists all filled their parts in most praiseworthy fashion, Dora Hope pleasing the audience greatly with "When the shadows homeward fly," and what seemed a difficult song for a boy in "Who is Sylvia?" being very capably taken by Neville Davies. In the costume and action songs the audience found great delight. The group of nymphs in "Fair Arcadee" were charmingly dressed, and ' were very clever in their rendering of this selection, while their reappearance was heartily I welcomed in " Hush ! here comes the dream man," the solo part of which was given with much simple grace by Ada Knight. The pre- , paration in both these items had been in the hands of Miss E. Brown. May Woodland won much applause with "When grandmamma was quite a little girl," and the party of quaintly and prettily dressed childisen in this number added to its attractiveness. Here the prepara- tion had been entrusted to Miss Broomhead and Miss White. Several very charming dances were given, the fruit of tuition by, Miss A. M. Wallington and Mrs. J. Whitehouse, whilst the artistic themes and graceful movements in " Dresden China" made it quite one of the con- tributions of the evening. In the Shakespearian ,/ coon song, "My Juliet," the responsibility for the production of which had been borne by '- ,Mr. Bowen, the minstrel boys gained golden opinions, and the solo part was dealt with in just the right way by G. H. Clubley. Recita- tions were forthcoming from 'Frank Dowling and Donald Dunbavand ; the former was very much at home in "His first long trousers, and Mark Twain or W. W. Jacobs could not have been more ,irresistibly cheerful than the latter in "A voyage of disaster." Dyson Whit- ham sang with an animation which brought 44-11711-111,1 ". The. Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the piano, and it goes without saying that the piano could n.et have been in better keeping. At the close of the evening, Councillor HENRY ROBERTS expressed on behalf of the managers of , the school, the teachers, and the general mem- bers of ,the audience, their thanks to the par- ents, who, by their willingness to provide the -- dresses, had made considerable sacrifice. He `believed that every parent Who had been pre- sent would feel that it had been worth while, and he was convinced that the influence of such an occasion as this upon the children would he felt in later years. Mr. Roberts recalled the fact that he was himself an old boy of the school, his earliest connection with it-going back over 55 years, and in a closing word of com- mendation he made reference to the highly esteemed character and work of the head master, Mr. Edward Wallington. For brightness and variety, for the high tone -;='! and perfect good taste of every item, and for success in sending everyone home in the best of spirits, the evening must be written aown a conspicuous achievement. All those who had a share both in preparation and in execution of the programme are to be heartily congratu- lated. It was an occasion worthy of the good name and reputation of the People's College.

div.head: Results of Examinations.
div.p: Results of Examinations.

Canon Morley Stevenson submitted to the Warrington Education Committee on Monday the results of the different -examinations in science, commercial, and other subjects. In certain subjects, he said, there appeared to be a falling off, but that was due to the Board of Education having altered the system of exam- iriation. The result in the cookery section could not have been surpassed. Out of 53 students 52 passed.

div.p: STOCKTON HEATH
TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.

The "Waits" have arrived. They did not wait until Christmas drew any nearer: They were Out on Saturday Dispensing seasonable melody. Playing very well they soon Found money rolling in abundantly. Residents pay while the "Waits" wait. Some did not want money—just yet. These "Waits" are waiting till Christmas Day. Messenger boys have now got out Their Christmas collecting books. These and other things. have convinced The Heathens that Christmas is truly coming. Do not ask who won the cup tie Up the Heath way if you value your life. There were dejected heathens on Saturday. An 8-goals to nil defeat takes a Very great deal of explaining away. Latchford has the laugh this time. If the mild weather continues Until Christmas Day a Heathen thinks , He Can gather enough blackberries To make a blackberry and apple pie, Two boys met on the Swing Bridge about 5.45 on Saturday. The first llOy, who had been in town, said, " Tommy, how have y gone on at the foot- .. ball match?" " Oh, they 'have lost !" said Billy. " Wno? Latchford?' inquired the, first. "No, silly ! Stockton Heath !" answered Billy. "What's the score?" queried the ignorant one. "Only 8 goals to nil!" came the anwer. ." Oh, eck ! What a whacking Solemnly the two passed on.
Death of a Resident.—A well-known resident in the person of Mr. William Richardson died at Holly Bank, Walton, on Wednesday. An account of his career will be found in another column.

That Swing Bridge.—Through the system now pursued in allowing pedestrians and vehicular traffic to enter upon the Swing Bridge after it has settled, there was a narrow escape from a serious accident. A little girl bound for school got in front of a motor ear, and but for the promptitude displayed by the motorist in jam. ming on the brakes she would have been run over. By the present system the bridge at cer- tain times is little short of a death-trap.

Garden Society Members Play.—The members of the Stockton Heath Garden Society held a bridge • and whist drive in the Hall Cafe on Thursday evening. The attendance was not so large as was expected, but the evening proved most enjoyable. The bridge prizes were won by Mr. 1). Howard and Mrs. Watson. Whist prize-winners were: Ladies-1, Mrs. Swinton; 2, "Mrs. Brooks; gentlemen—l, Mr. Spinks; 2, Miss Swinton, who played as a gentleman.

Tramps Avoid the Heath.—" It's not safe to walk through Cheshire," was the comment of an elderly tramp named William Kimber, who was charged with begging at Stockton Heath, after he had been sentenced to 14 days' "hard" at the Occasional Court. 'lnspector Meese inti- mated that the prisoner had a very had opinion of Cheshire, for he said that it was the wdrst county he had ever visited: He had paid the county three visits and each time, he alleged, he had been unfairly locked up.

Christmas Shopping.—Stockton-Ifeath'tra&s-' men will in no way be left behind in making an attractive display for the ilithriStmas shop ping. We ask our readers' attention to the really choice selection of fancy and useful articles exhibited by Messrs. A. Faulkner, Lon- don-road. :Messrs. Moore and Co., chemists, offer perfumery, fancy soaps, toilet requisites,. all of which make most acceptable presents. For the inner man, the display of poultry, game, fish, &c., by Messrs. Morris, London-road, speaks for itself. Comment would be super- fluous. Hayes Bros and Mr. Prince, of London- road, are saving busy housewives much worry. Their show of seasonable toothsome, dainties is all that could be desired. '"The kind that mother makes."

The Sewers: An Explanation.—At the last meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Com- mittee, a question as to the adoption of the water carriage system in substitution of the pail system was discussed. Mr. Ashton, the clerk, was explaining that the water system had been adopted in Runcorn at an estimated cost of £7 per house and was working very satisfac- torily. Mr. Whitley asked whether the sewers Runcern'had csUfficient‘capactty fort dealing with all the matter going through them, and the answer was "Yee." Our report made it appear that this remark referred to the capacity of the Stockton Heath sewers. As a matter of fact, the Stockton Heath sewers, which were laid 30 years ago, when there were only a few houses in the parish, are not at present of the necessary capacity, and to make them so would entail a considerable expenditure.

Youngsters "Joy Day."—there Was joy in the village mission room on Saturday, when happy children, exhibiting smiling and flushed faces. packed the prettily—arranged Parish Room. It was the children's annual treat, and, as usual, they made' the best of it. In the centre was a large, well-laden Christmas tree, and around this the little ones gathered with longing eyes focussed upon one, or perhaps more, of the-dang- ling dainties, and they appeared to show a spirit of patience. by standing there until they were kindl,Y told that later the tree would be shorn of all its glory for their sakes. This pacified them, and -round and round they rambled, stop- ping here and there at one or other of the stalls, which formed an acceptable border to the room. but they ever had an eye on the giant tree which overshadowed all else. Towards the close of the happy event the Vicar, assisted by- a number of ladies, deprived Santa Clans of one of his tasks by themselves presenting the many pretty arti- cles to the children.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

A Nurse Complains.._-Margaret Plumpton, a nurse, Victoria-terrace, Penketh, at the War- rington County Sessions on Wednesday, com- plained about the bad state of the Warrington- road, Penketh, on the pathway of which she had ridden. The roads, she said, were in a filthy condition. She was going to see a patient, and if she had been in a dirty state she would. have been 'reported to the Midwives' Board. She was "between the devil and the deep sea."—A fine of 2s. 6d. was imposed.—pefendant : I am quite willing to pay, but wish you would see to the roads.

Thought It a Practical Joke.—Atthe Warring- ton County Sessions on Wednesday, Edward Mnrphy, Chapel-road, Penketh, was summoned for having ridden a bicycle on the footpath.— The officer stated that when ho saw defendant the latter said: Are you the man I ran into yesterday?"—Defendant said he thought the man, was. playing a practical joke, as the officer was not in uniform. The road was very bad and he had skidded twice. How did a man recognise a policeman in 'plain clothes?—Super- intendent Foster: A man has no right to ride Oil the .footpath.—The Chairman, Mr. W. P. Rylands: Have the general public the power to sta a man?—Superintendent Foster: Yes.—A fine of ss. was imposed.

div.head: O! ? FORD.
div.p: O! ? FORD.

Social.-1 very successful social was held in Orford School on Friday. Dancing and games were -indulged in, and Mr. J. Swinton acted as M.C. Songs were rendered by Miss S. E. Swin- ton, "Down the vale"; Mr. J. Gibson, "When the ebb-tide flows," "Jack's the boy," and, in re- sponse to an encore, "Rosary"; and Mr. H. Plumpton, "Bandolero," "Muleteer of Main- gar," and "Red Wing" (encore). Mrs. R. G. Brandreth accompanied - and played for danc- ing. The proceeds were devoted to the fund for providing music for the choir..

div.head: GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL.

Let There be Light.—At the Rural District Council meeting a Dutton on Tuesday, a letter was read from the Grappenhall Parish Council; with reference to the erection of a street lamp in ' Chester-road. The Parish Council passed the following resolution: "That a gas lamp be fixed on the Cheiter-road at the corner of Barrymore- road."—Councillor Lister Kaye said such a pro- vision had become necessary owing to the mak- ing of new streets. There were a good many motor cars came round the corner, and it was necessary that a lamp should .be fixed there.— The Council decided to act in the matter.

A Squabble Echo.—An echo of the recent squabble over the Grappenhall sewerage scheme was heard at the Runcorn Rural District Coun- cil meeting on Tuesday, when Mr. Lister Kaye said: I was here a month ago, and amongst other things I said "There was a unanimous vote to go for a cheaper scheme." Mr. Pilling said he never voted. In your own minutes, Mr. Clerk, of September 30th, you have, " Resolved, with Councillor Lister Kaye dissenting, that the Chairman and Clerk attend at the Local Gov- ernment Board inquiry," &c.—The Clerk: Coun- cillor Pilling, was presiding that day, and the chairman's vote is not recorded.—Councillor Lister Kaye: If he had dissented it would have been.—The Clerk: Yes.—Councillor Pilling: I have spoken the truth. Old Scholars' Association.—The fourth annual reunion in connection with the ,Grappenhall Old Scholars' Association was held in, the Grap- .penhall Schoolroom- on Saturday evening, when a large number of old scholars and friends spent a very enjoyable time together. Mr. W. 11. Wooding, a- manager of the school, presided in the unfortunate absence of Mr. T: Parr, who arrived later in the evening. A very attractive programme was provided, which included solos and duets, vocal and instrumental quartets, and part songs, while old school songs were sung with •much enthusiasm. A character sketch, "Uncle John from Yorkshire," caused consider- able amusement. The catering was efficiently carried out by Mr. Woodcock. The whole pro- ceedings reflected credit on the committee, who were responsible for such -a pleasurable even- ing.

div.head: LANCASHIRE'S "GREED."
div.p: LANCASHIRE'S "GREED."

Protest Against Annexation. The proposal of the Lancashire County Coun- cil to extend thoir boundary is going to be strongly protested against from Cheshire. The Runcorn Council again discussed the matter on Tuesday. -

Mr. Woodward characterised the appeal as an attempt at pilfering. The discussion arose on the following. The joint Parliamentary Committees of the Runcorn Union and Guardians having consid- ered the representations by the Lancashire County Council to the Local Government Board for an alteration of the boundaries of Lanca- shire and Cheshire, under which certain por- tions of the parish of Grappenhall and The!- wall within the area of the Rural Council and Runcorn Union would be transferred to the county of Lancashire, it was resolved that it be pointed out to the Board and Council that if the application be successful there would be transferred from this Union and Council an area of about 550 acres; a population of about 260, and a ratable value of .0,140, whilst there would be added to the parish of Thelwall 16 acres and a ratable .-value of £4. That the Board of Guardians and Rural District Council be recommended to proceed in active opposition to the proposals, and to authorise their com- mittee to take such action either independently or with other Councils or Boards, as they may find necessary:- That-. Messrs. Woodward, Lin.- aker, sell., Pilling, Lister Kaye and E. Hewitt be appointed as a Joint Committee to carry out the resolution.
Attempts_ at Pilfering.

Mr. Woodward said.. he thought that the appeal of the Conntyof Lancastei was an- other of, those seriotts *tempts at pilfering im- portantbecoming a little too common. There had been a former attempt, but it had not succeeded, and he felt that in their own interests it was in- cumbent upon them to put all their efforts forth so that the present appeal should nof -he suc- cessful. The proposal -would Mean a decrease to them of £628 per year from Thelwall and Grappenhall, and the 16 acres it was proposed to give them would only mean per year re- turn. They stood to lose £627 per year on the basis of 4s. per annum rate. Another thing in that connection was that in the application pnt before them half the canal was included in the claim, in so far as the base of their area was concerned. Up to and beyond that point men- tioned the whole of the canal was in their area. If Lancashire got one half they would take half the, traffic with it. The committee strongly recommended the Council to take ur an attitude of strong opposition to the scheme. He moved the adoption of the report. Mr. Morris seconded.
Mr. Linaker said the proposition was to abstract 929 acres with a ratable value of £9,160, and give in return 217 acres'with a ratable value of £7Bl. _

"Get An Aeroplane." Mr. Lister Kaye said that if Lancashire did get to their area they had no way except by the wooden bridge over the Mersey to get to it. Mr. Morris: They might get an aeroplane and fly over. (Laughter.) - Mr. Lister Kaye: I support what Mr. Wood- ward has said.

Mr. Woodward said the matter was important in view of the sewerage scheme before the three parishes. If that Portion- stated were taken from them the sewerage scheme would • fall heavily on other parishes. (Hoar, hear.) Mr. PilLing proposed. and Mr. Mclntyre sec- onded that the report be adopted. The Board of Guardians passed.a similar reso- lution.

div.head: HIGH ILEGur,
div.p: HIGH ILEGur,
Tale of a Tail Light.—At the Petty Sessions at Lymm on Wednesday, John Isaac, of 20, Cros- field-street, Warrington, was charged with fail-

jag to have a lighted lamp attached to the rear of his motor car in Warrington-road, High Legh, on November 17. The local police . evidence showed that at 2;45 on the morning of Novem- ber 17 the rear light was not burning.—Defend7 ant 'Stateil to the Bench that he had been-inte Derbyshire, and was returning to Warrington. It was a very light night, but it was windy. He had stopped for some purpose or other in the vicinity of the " Kilton," • and then the light was burning, and he used it again after the officer had stopped him.—He was fined 24: 6d., including costs.
LINES FROM LYMM.

At last—Punctuality. .7 The. Councillors learned .the value of time At the last Council meeting of the year. They commenced the business on "the Knock." Indeed, the reporters were the culprits. • On Thursday they were a few minutes behind. The Councillors had the laugh, And the reporters took it all in good part, As members appear to have taken it. Nothing like ending the old year well. Complaints may be made of the gas, But, according to the Rector, it has extra- ordinary illuminative powers. On Thursday he declared that he got a dull, red glow, By which he could see nothing. Even with a powerful microscope We have never been able to see nothing. lie meant to .say he could not see anything. Councillor Dixon • cannot attend for several months, As illness prevents him. We should ,not like him to; resign, And many Lyromites think the same.

Rum mag e Sal e.—Considerable success favoured the rummage sale held last Saturday in the Lymm Parochial School. At the sale, which was organised by the Rector (the Rev. G. B. Thurston), a varied collection of articles were displayed.
Toys For Hospital.--At a meeting of the Lymna Council Sanitary Committee it was resolved that the thanks of the Council be•given to Mr. Wat- kins for his gift of books, toys, &c.., for the hospital.

Pastor's Death.—The _ Rev. Wilson 'Barrett passed away suddenlY at his residence, 11S, Saltergate, Chesterfield, at the age of 72. The interment took place at Chesterfield Cemetery. Mr. Barrett was the father of the recent pastor of the Lymm Congregational Church.

Celluloid Dangers.—The Sanitary Committee of the Lymm Council have resolved that the Clerk be instructed to obtain copies of poster calling attention to the inflammable nature of celluloid articles to the number of 100, and that David Daniels be instructed to distribute same. The Council confirmed this.

Members of the Council.—Conneillor S. Davies presided at the meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council. There were also present: Councillors T. Warburton, W. G. Groves, R. 11. Gotobed, G. L. Welford, 0. G. Smith and W. Gould, Rev. G. B. Thurston; with Messrs. D. Mullard (clerk), D. Mort (surveyor), C. I. Barnes (water manager), W. L. Donaldson (gas manager).

Invalid Councillors.—At the Council meeting on Thursday letters were read from Councillors T. P. W. Dixon and F. Lockyer thanking the Council for their expressions of sympathy and best wishes for speedy recovery. Councillor Dixon wrote and said it would be several months before he could attend any meeting, and he felt those who had elected him would be acting quite fairly if they allowed him to resign, al- though he would be sorry to do so.

Broom Edge Horticulturiits.—ln the '"lance sheet of the Broom Edge and District Horticul- tural Show, the Honorary Secretary, Mr. E. Landless, reports ti successful annu- 1 meeting, which was held under the presidency ' Mr. W. 3ould. The Treasurer's report was. a very satis- factory one, showing a profit of ..,C8 14s. gd. on the exhibition, making a total balance in hand of £l4 3s. 31d. The committee were re-elected en bloc.

Lighter Side of Politics.--A well-attended cmoking concert was held in the Conservative Club Assembly Room on Wednesday night. Mr. R. Oliver presided. Mr. J. Rabbitt and Mr. J. Poole. both of Warrington, Contributed some enjoyable songs in their best style. Mr. Franklyn Taylor. of Timperley, a favourite entertainer with Lymm audiences, was as popu- lar as ever. Local talent was represented by Messrs. H. Gibbon, E. Morris and G. H. Parker.

Grammar School Concert.—There was a capi- tal attendance of parents, friends and old scholars at the Grammar School on Saturday evening, on the occasion of the School Christmas concert. The principal item on the programme was the children's play, "Queen of the May," which was received with marked approval, the acting of the youthful performers being excel- lent and the costumes very pretty. Other con- tributions to a most enjoyable evening were small Latin and French plays, and violin solos by ,

Independent Methodists.—For the purpose of assisting the Church and Restoration Funds), a 'nubile tea and concert were held at Sion Chapel, Cherry-lane, on Wednesday evening. The attendance at the tea was so good that extra accommodation had to bo made for.. persons 'desirous of participating in the choice ediNia nrovided by the lady members of the chapel. After tea a miscellaneous concert was given, contributed presidency of Mr. W. Mort, who also a couple of readings. Pianoforte solos were played by Miss Marion Hewitt and Mr. H. T. - Mercer.-the latter being a proficient accompanist for the evening. Songs were ably rendered by Miss Jones, Messrs. Bibby, J. Ellis a.nd a Okell. Miss Allen gave some interesting and clever recitations.

For the Sailormen.—The value of the Mer- chant Seamen Service to this country was em- nhasised at a lecture given in the Lymm Drill Hall on Monday night by the Rev. D. W. Rob- gym, chaplain to the Mersey Mission to Seamen. The Rev. G. B. Thurston, presided. The Chair- man said he had known the Mission for 25 years Ind had been well acquainted with former chap- lains. It was not a missionary society, in the meaning in which this was generally understood but it was a society in which the Church wished to stretch out a brotherly and helpful hand to the seamen when they came to port. The lec- turer said that people did not generally -realise tiuit the Merchant Service was quite as much a national service as were the Army and Navy, for they were quite as dependent upon one as the other. Further, the Merchant Service had been' the means of • developing England from a• small unimportant island into a great world- wide Empire: This being the case, it was only right they should cater for the spiritual well- being of the men in that service.

Women Liberals.—On Thursday night the Lyn= and District Women's Liberal Associa- lion held a well-attended meeting in the Primi- tive Methodist Schoolroom. -- Mr. James Rad- cliffe, who was in the -chair, expressed his regret that the appointed speaker,'Mr. Walter Davies, was unable to be present, owing to an engage- 'ment in London on an important insurance case. However, they were-fortunate in securing the services of Mr. Wood, Who was also an authority on the subject of insurance. Mr., Wood con- lined his address wholly to the National Insur- ,ance Act. He said that he Was not present as party politician, and therefore spoke about the Act from a non-party view. The speaker dealt at length on the sanatoria benefits, after which he described the working of the Act in its rela- tion to domestic servants, teachers, and others. How National Insurance affected the Compen- sation Act and other points were mentioned. Questions being invited, an exhilarating discus- sion took place, which served to clear up a number of points upon which several members of the audience appeared to be under some mis- cOnception.

The Justices.—At the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday the Bench was composed of the Hon. J. E. Cross, Major Groves, and Messrs. T. J. Ridgway, J. Coson and S. W. Gould. Scene at a School.—At 'the Petty Sessions on Wednesday, John Griffiths, of the. Rookery, Lymm, was charged with failing to send his daughtei Caroline to school. The evidence given by the Attendance Officer (Mr. H. T. Mercer), and Miss Innes and Mrs. Ditchfield, head mistress and assistant teacher respectively of the Lymm Girls' School. showed that between October 27th and December 2nd the school had been opened 48 times, but the...child had only been present on 18 occasions. The child...._they alleged, attended school most unclean in both her clothes and personal appearance. The girl had been naughty on the day before her absence, and her teacher, bringing her to the front of the class, had remarked, it WAS alleged, "that

the child, besides being untidy, was also set- ting a bad example." The mother visited the school at the dinner interval and said she would serve Mrs. Duckworth as she had served a teacher ,in the Potteries. It was the -duty of a teacher to report unclean scholars.—Defend- ant's wife, for the defence, denied saying what she was alleged to have said to the teacher,- and gave as an excuse for the child's nbn-attendance that she was not going to have the child in- sulted.—The Chairman said she had no right to keep the child from school, and she had no right to use a threat against the teacher. It cost her nothing for education, and she must use soap and water to keep the child clean.—A fine of 2s. Gd., including costs, was imposed.

div.head: TIIE ECCENTRIC
div.p: TIIE ECCENTRIC
An Improvement Reported.

There seems to have been an improvement in regard to the gas of the district, which was com- plained about at the last meeting of the Coun- cil. On Thursday evening Coun. Warburton said he noticed fronla report that one of the mem- bers had complained of bad gas. Since the last meeting the service had been overhauled and he would like to know whether there had been any improvement. He thought it was not the gas of the district, but the service. It was not fair to try and " set on" the Gas Department, as people had been doing at the present time. . .

.11e'Rev. G.. B. Thurston: You should sit underneath the gas. Councillor Warburton asked if any fault could be found with the street lamps. If the street lamps were right it must be the service that was wrong. The Chairman: The gas now seems bettar all .round. The Rev. G. B. Thurston: The drawback was that there was an 'accumulation in the service pipe. Such a lot of stuff comes with the gas. which should be taken out, or it will block up the pipes. Nfr. Donaldson: In your case it was. ...The , obstruction was an accumulation of rust. Thes2 can be set right.

div.head: Lights Still Dance.
div.p: Lights Still Dance.

The Rev. G. B. Thurston: There is an im- provement in the illumination, but the light.s still go up and down, although it does not go out as it did. It palpitates considerably, as if the pressure were not even. Before the altera- tion I used to get a dull, red glow, by which I could not see anything. Councillor Warburton said the people would find that a few shillings for the local plumber would be well spent. The Rev. G. B. Thurston said there was some- thing wrong with the purification; the gas was not properly cleansed. It was dirty gas. • Mr. Donaldson: There is some trouble with the tar.

Councillor Smith: I suppose if you got a new purifier it would 'reme(ly- th% matter. . Councillor Gotobed thought it was about time the Council decided to do something to thq plant. They wanted a new plant. The Council should therefore tackle the matter. Councillor Smith: It is only just now that we find ourselves in a position to do El). - Mr. Donaldson: We have only had a new washer since I have been here. The matter then dropped.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Striking Pictures.—Padgate Nonconformists were placed under an obligation to their Lymm friends when on Tuesday evening they were entertained to splendid tableaux vivants in the Padgate Wesley Hall. The Rev. E. Morgan pre- sided, and explained that the artistes were -ama- teurs. All the performers were giving their services gratis, and that made them all the more grateful to their neighbouring friends. The entertainment was versatile, hut the outstanding feature was the representations . of , statuary. Some of the scenes were most effective, and the audience showed appreciation by applause. The artistes wore Mesdames Margetts and Egerton, Misses Pearson, Hazlehurst, W. Morris, E. Eger- ton, and Winstafiley, Messrs. Egerton, Ingle- -field, Margetts, F. :Brciwn: And Hinten, and Master Eric. Hudson. The pictures were "Two's company, three's none," "Rosary," "Kiss first," "Faith, hope and charity;"_" Summer, or a dream-of fair women," "f 915 or the -new woman," "Christmas Eve," "Darby And Joan," "Pear's soap," "Two strings to her bow," "Rock of ages;" and "Rule, Britannia." ..1V pianoforte duet,-which added to the evening's enjoyment, was given by Mrs. Margetts, and Mr. H. S. Brown and the latter supplied the subsequent -accompaniments to ,songs, which were rendered between the various tableaux.l Mr. Hudson and Mrs. H. S. Brown were capable workers in the staging of the performance.

div.head: BUILDER AND GIRL.
div.p: BUILDER AND GIRL.
Paduale Case Dismissed.

The adjourned case in which Rodtselen Lodge, Ivy Cottage, Tidal-lane, Padgatt applied for an order against James A. liougi ton, builder, Greystones; Padgate-lane, came u for resumed hearing at the Warriftton• Coun' Sessions on Wednesday, before Mr. W. Rylands and other magistrates.

It will be remembered that at the previou. hearing the girl alleged that the offences com- plained of took place in March, but on Wednes- day Mr. Houghton proved an alibi; and the case was dismissed. In regard to the alleged fraud by means of. .a letter, the magistrates found that these had not been proved. In his evidence Mr. Houghton said he was never near the house any time in March. The first time he ever saw the girl was the 21st May The girl's statements as to the alleged offences were untrue. On March 11th he went to see the international football match at Wrexham. He stayed • with his brother-in-law until the 16th March. Whilst he was •working at the house in May the mother and two sisters were there all the time. He never introduced Riding to the girl as Russell. The girl told him she had had a postcard from Russell, and he said "Mr. Russell?" She replied "Yes, you remember, that gent. from Liverpool." He (witness) did not give him away. When Mr. Lodge saw him on the morning that the child was born, Mr. Lodge said that his daughter had given birth

to a child, and that she accused him (Mr' .Houghton) of having something to do with it. Lodge said his daughter was dying, and he (Wit- ness) said "She will not die with that lie 05 her lips." He went to the house with the father, and on the way Lodge said if people got to know about the matter it would do him (Houghton) a great amount of harm, and that people with daughters and servants would ot have him near.

"To Pay a Small Sum." Lodge said it would be better for him to PaY a small amount of money, rather than anything coming out. He (witness) said he would not pay any money. When they got to the bedrooto he found that the doctor was not there, and realised that he had been trapped. lie teld th@i. girl she was telling lies, and that if she had been in the condition she was he v.- 3uld have wrung her neck. In an interview N th Lodgei downstairs he refused to pay an3-t .ing, en( he said, "If Lodge did not apologise by Monde morning I would sue him for blackmail." Lodge then asked him to see Riding and see if he could get £250. He told Lodge that the whole thing was a swindle, and that he would have nothing to do with it. When they went to Liverpool Lodge paid hll expenses.

An Apology. The apology was drawn up and signed, int, a newspaper would not publish it until it hau been attested by a solicitor. He showed it t° dozens of people in Fearnhtad. He showed the.' apology to Turner, who %aid he knew severs,' men who had been with the girl. He had never offered Turner £lOO to say he had been With the girl. Turner refused to come as a witness' ' The girl knew he was a married man, for his boy- had brought his dinner and tea. C'ros,_,-examined by Mr. Burgis, defendant stated that he had never indulged in 0•10 familiarity with the complainant. He kn i ef Riding was innocent when he went to LiverPne„; They went to Liverpool so that things shoui" be mutually -arranged. Mr. Burgis : Although you knew there was 11° liability on his part? Witness continued that he was not 1.01301" sible for bringing Riding and the girl together' When Lodge came to see him on the 14th Decenl- ber it was suggested that Riding was the fatlle! of the child. He went to see the girl to get hi° character cleared, and that was the only reason - She did not say he was the father of the child when they were in the bedroom. Henry Ewins, employed by Harland and Wolf!. Liverpool, said that on one occasion in Mare° defendant stayed with him for the week follow- ing the international match.

The Alibi. Mr. Arthur Ward, formerly in partnershiP with Houghton, said the time sheets had nel'eir been out of his possession since he receive° them. It was the 26th March when he -and Mr' Bennett went through Ivy Cottage, where the girl lived, to see what wanted doing, anda,hb: sent Turner down to put in two sashes. time sheet for the week ending April showed the only work done at the house thav year. Houghton was travelling up and down the country that year, trying to get a, patent In the market, and he never did any joinery w°r The only period when Houghton worked there was May 21st. Cross-examined by Mr. Burgis, witness sai they had not kept a proper wage-book.

At this point the caie v;:las stopped . The Chairman said the Bench had come to t_Alle decision that the charges of fraud had fatk; and by the evidence of witnesses and docureen,e an alibi had been proved. The case would " dismissed.

div.p: RUNCORN GUARDIANS.
!The Insurance Act -Question.

'l'he fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn :Board of Guardians was held at _Dutton on Tuesday, Mr. J. It Jones (vicehairinan) pre- siding. The Clerk said that a joint meeting Of the .Parliamentary Committees of the Council and Guardians met that morning, Mr. Woodward ipregiding. Having consic,lered a resolution from The Steyning Union, the Union's ConimiUce resolved: "That the Guardians of the 11Uncorn limion are unanimously of the opinion that certain sections of the National Insurance Act 7are unsatisfactory and unfair in their applica- tion to Poor Law Institutions, inasmuch as, without definite prospect of reimbursement, *Guardians of the Poor, under existing condi- tion, are legally liable to receive into their institutions certain insured persons who may ,have become temporarily incapable of following their employment through sickness i or prospect of maternity, and they would therefore respect- fully urge that the National Insurance Act should he amended so as to provide that any sick or maternity benefit which woukl in the ordinary course accrue to fully insured persons under the Act, and who shall become inmates .of a Poor Law Institution, shall be paid to the 'Guardians during the period the insured per- -sons referred to remain chargeable to the com- mon fund. The report was adopted.

div.head: COUNCIL AND CONSUNIPTIoN.
div.p: COUNCIL AND CONSUNIPTIoN.
Preventative Steps to be Taken.

Mr. C. E. Linaker presided at the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural District Council on Tuesday. The Tuberculosis Committee reported as fol- lows: The Council - are prepared to pay the cost of a bacteriological examination of sputum of persons suspected • of being tubercular. They also 'agree to pay the cost of the necess'ary vessels for taking ,specimens of sputum, and to provide spitoons. That circu- lars with advice concerning steps to he taken to prevent the spread of the disease, and of the use and composition of goods for tubercular patients be delivered 'by the Medical Officer of Health in his areas- in which cases have been iiotified." That placards be posted from time to time in the Council's area giving advice against spitting and Concerning the value of, fresh air and cleanliness, and that notices warning people against spitting be posted in common lodging- houses, factories, bakeries, workshops, hackney carriages, and other places frequented by the public. That arrangements be • 'made for periodical disinfection at intervals of three months of rooms used by tubercular patients, and that no action be taken regarding the provi- sion of shelters for tubercular patients until the intention of the" County Council has been ascer- tained." On the proposition of Councillor Woodward the report was adopted.

he death of an elderly stranger in the Work- house somehow recalled the case of a foundling that came under my notice in a union in which I lived some years. Evidently of triunp parent- age, the little one was found lying in the street and was removed to the workhouse. It was unable to talk, and came to be .called simply "Dick." A's the lad grew it Was evident that he was an imbecile, and ultimately he was taken to the county asylum. I accompanied a depu- tation of local Guardians on their annual visit to that institution, and so made. his acquaint- ance. lie always appeared on their list as "Dick (unknown)." He died at, the age of 22, having cost the Board a substantial sum for maintenance. Those who had deserted him were never traced; apparently they were quite indifferent as to .his -fate. 14 the course of the years I have known of several Strangers who have died and been buried without disclosing their identity, so that it has been impossible to communicate with their friends—supposing they had any. Here is the sort of material with whicit many a romance has been woven.

Lifeboat Service. - On Thursday evening, in connection With Eli:. Warrington branch, a remarkable effort was made in behalf Of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution—which, by the way, was founded by lioyal Charter in 1824. The last available report states that .during the previous year no fewer than 759 lives were saved by lifeboats be- longing .to the institution, making a total of 50,824 persons rescued—since its inception in 1824. The number of lifeboats constituting the institution's fleet is 277. It costs roughly about £lOO,OOO per. annum to maintain the service in 4. thorough state of efficiency, the administra- tion expenses being about- 8 per cent. One of the features of the year 1912 was the addition of a number of motor lifeboats, which have proved to be quite satisfactory. That such a charity should vainly appeal for adequate support is unthinkable. True it is that no British heart will consent to depreciate the dauntless courage of our brave sailor ancestors who made our Empire master of the seas; vet is there not a leeper pleasure in :honouring and supporting. the beneficent heroism displayed by the brave fellows who man our lifeboats?

div.head: P.S.A.
div.p: The P.S.A.

The open meeting of the Warrington P.S.A. in the Park Picture Palace on Sunday afternoon reminded .me of something said by the Rev. Silvester Horne, M.P., in view of the National Conference in Manchester. He admitted that it was unconventional, but argued that it was an enduring movement. He gave it as his own ex- perience that Boman Catholics, Anglicans, Free Churchmen, and nailtitudes of the great denom- ination of No-Churchmen and of almost every nationality—French, German, Austrian, Rus- sian, and the rest—have existed in closest in- timacy in one Brotherhood organisation. Re- ferring. to its genial theology; he went on "Rut our critics complain that we are not reverent: We laugh and we ,cheer, and we occasionally interject questions or objections. 'We d 0... If tears are reverent, why is laughter irreverent? If we may express our sadness, why 110 t our gladness? If we may sing hallelujah, why mast we not say Hear, hear!' ? Why is silence reverent and audible expression of interest irreverent? Were Chrysostom's congregations irreverent when they burst into applause? Was the vest audience in Westminster. Abbey irreverl' ent when it shouted 'God save the King and • Hurrah r at the Coronation service? As for the humour at our meetings, it is 'sometimes, I admit, as crude 'as much of the theology in our Churches ; but it is, I think, kindly and genial, and I never can see that humour, which is rare, is less'reverent than .the lack of it, which is abundant:'
"The Messiah."

In all the region round about local perform-, ances of *extracts from this seasonable oratorio are being given, .the Most important one thus far being that at Legh-Street Primitive Metho- diSt Church last ,Sunday. An old colleague of mine, who has developed into a superior sort of person in a musicaj sense, writes: "Within the last generation, the striUly musical world has almost freed itself from Han- delian influence, and is .now in a position to critically estirnate, Hqnders. position -amongst the giants of music. Handel is still a national fetish with thousands of English people, who could not. for their lives when listening to

' Israel in Egypt' hear any difference of -quality between ait 'effort, of ,geilius‘ like "The people- -Ji ill 1 f_! r , and hack -work such is Their ,land brought forth frogs.' fhe reaction of modern- minded cultured musicians against 'Handel- adoration has progressed rapidly, and has, per- haps, gone too far,. for.his greatness lies deep while his faults are on the surface, and leap to the eyes of everyone not blinded by tradition and religious associations. Soon after the death of •llandel, English 'oratorio music en- tered on 'a century of artistic darkness over which brooded from first to last the 'colossal Shadow of the great Anglo-German, and only in recent years have.we discovered that our long night is over. If English music had to be crushed, if it was necessary to bow the knee for all that time to one single work, perhaPS, after all 'The Messiah' was our wisest choice."
The Christmas. Spirit. Another old colleague of mine was wont to write in this strain on the reeurrence of Christ- ina:

"What is the use of wishing a friend or neigh- bour a merry Christmas in a mere perfunctory manner, much less in. a grudging sour spirit which belies the wish? What is the good of wishing anybody a merry Christmas if no effort is being made to make it mirthful? Words are of no use; even deeds may,fail. it is the spirit 1 which must make the Christmas a :merry one. And the spirit will not rest at words if deeds are possible. Happiness cannot be self-con tained. It is never selfish. It grows on What it gives rather than what it gcts." . In this connection one, is inevitably reminded of Dickens and Washington Irving. Of the former we are sure to hear a good :tieal during the next week or So. It lt as the latter who wrote (inter alia): 't Amidst the general call to happiness, the bustle, of the spirits, and stir of the affections,' which prevail at this period, what bosom can remain insensible? It is, indeed, the season of regenerated feeling—the season for kindling. not merely the tire of hospitality in the hall, but the genial Ilanie °of charity in the heart; the scene of early love again rises green to'memory beyond the sterile waste of years; and the idea of home, fraught with the fragrance of home- dwelling joys, reanimates the drooping spirit, as the Arabian breeze will sometimes waft the freshness of the distant fields to the weary pil- grims of the desert." -

div.head: Good Cheer.
div.p: Good Cheer.

This, of course, includes the enjoyment of the lest: of creature comforts in the company of coi. genial spirits—the promotion of' good fellowship, pre-eminentiy and emphatically. Christmas is the season when families gather round the home hearth, when friend's clasp hand's in loving communion, when the absent ones return to the old roof, when goodwill prevails, If that be not at the root of our Christmas pleasure, then is Yuletide merriment a failure and a mockery. I suppose that anyone not in the trade can have no conception of the prepara- tions 'going on, not only in this country, bur tn many of ,the principal countries of Europe, llussia not excluded, for many months before- hand with the view- of supplying the British Christmas market. Take the simple case of the lordly and more or less exotic turkey, Which has- of late years well-nigh -supplanted the time- honoured, if indigestible, goose. The latter, though so hardy and easily reared in our changeful climate, is, and 'has for some lime , decidedly been, at a discount, as compared with 1 the other. See how this works out. I read that I

turkey breeding has never made any 'great hetahvay in this country, nothing really sail- ;cient .to bring the supply up to the demand. llence the warmer countrieS—Soulhern France, Lower Switzerland, Italy and Southern Bussia —cark more than compete-with us successfully, and dnnually -ponr shiploads of these delicacies into the British market. To be sure, the bill hag to -be paid. It is not small. What with eggs, fowls, turkeys and other matters of a similar nature, the annual account just amounts to the tidy little sum of about twenty millions sterling. So says my authority, and it gives one furiously to think. Concerning Santa Claus.

According to the Bev. D. Smythe Palmer, whose article on ,the subject I have in a back number of the "Nineteenth Century," this legend, strangely enough, seems to have arisen out of ' an exaggerated view of the sterner aspect ,of, the most popular saint of the Middle Ages—St, Ni.cholas .(Bishop of Myra in the fOurth century). - ()Wing to his extraordinary piety in infancy Nicholas ,had been adopted as the patron saint of children. The pretty legend which told how the good Bishop stealthily flung a • purse of gold through a window on three successive occasion, in order to proVide a mar- -1 riage portion for the: three fair daughters of a poverty-stricken geptleman in his- native : city, was so widely current that parents in later times pretended that the little presents which they provided for their children, at Christmas time had, been left by St. Nicholas (or Nicklas), who had popped in through the windows during the night. The 'perennial popularity of Santa Claus (i.e., Klaus, " Klas, the mutilated rem- nant of Nikolaus ") as the unseen giver of: Christmas gifts still keeps his memory green. Fathers and mothers, thus finding m Maul ally in St. Nicholas, in encouraging youthful virtue, after a time came to the judicious conclusion

that the patron saint of childhood ought pro- perly to be a terror to evil-doers, as weli as a rewarder of them that do well. Accordingly they provided him with a rod to be used when necessary. . . Nickel is used similarly iii German for a goblin or devil. In Sweden a worthless ore, which yielded no metal, used to he called "Kupfer-nickel" (or Kupfer-nicol, 1728), i.e., "copper-demon," whence comes our "nickel," as a name for a well-known base metal, as if produced by the mocking imps of the mine.

div.head: ME oßicin OF " CHRISTIANS, AWAKE."
div.p: ME oßicin OF " CHRISTIANS, AWAKE."
A Popular Xmas Hymn and Tune and How They
Were Written.

div.head: FAMOUS XMAS MORNING AT KERSALL CELL.
div.p: A FAMOUS XMAS MORNING AT KERSALL CELL.

Christmas brings, among many other things, the revival of a famous hymn. It would hardly be Christmas without it, and, unless our judg- ment is woefully defective in the matter of pOpiilar anisical taste, our children's children will hear it as regularly and gratefully as we do. "Christians, awake," is a stirring hymn, awl it is Nt to a noblq tune. What the hymn may owe to the tune for its popularity We do not profess to know. They were joined at the beginning for better or worse. We have never heard them apart, nor do we expect to do: • Let good folks hear the story of both, that they may bestow, 0i Christmas comes and goes, some fitting gratitude upon the memory of their worthy authors. - THE BYROM'S OF MANCIIFStiiI. -

Two hundred years ago there lived in Manchester an Edward Byrom, known to his friends ti's' prosperous- cloth Inerehant, and the father Of tWo bright boys. Those who explore 'the remaining fragment of Mitigate, known as Poets', Corner," may see a part of the city with which his two boys would be very familiar, for the Manchester Grammar School had its home there, as it has to-day, though housed, of course, in a more ancient and less commodious building. To the .:Grammar School Edward and John Byrom daily made their way. ,Edward wa-s to follow his father in the business of cloth merchant and was to be trained accordingly. John was the younger and eared little for business. His ,instinct was for literature, and Very early' in, life he tasted the best of- it. • As we are chiefly interested in John Byrom we will follow him from Manchester to Cam- bridge, for his father could afford to lavish money upon the education of his sons, and John was able to spend several years at the University.. Not that the elder 13yrom was extravagant. Indeed, there are letters extant which suggest something different. When, for instance, -John recorded that he had Paid a guinea to the hairdressers of Cambridge for a stylish wig, his father regarded it as an un- warrantable extravagance, and told him. that he might. have had his sister's cast-off hair. Which would have had the merit of being both genuine and cheap. But John was not a.fop. Ile was counted clever, and after qualifying as a physiciari„and completing study, went for a time as a surgeon to. Montpelier. The death of his father brought changes. The elder brother succeeded to the estate and John ,was obliged to mark out a course in life for himself and set about the darning ,of his own living.. With a skill that revealed him to be a Man of first-rate brain power, lie perfected a system of shorthand and devoted himself to teaching it. Ile married his cousin, took up abode in.a house near to the Manchester Grammar School, and spent some fruitful and industrious years as tutor of short- hand.

' lie had been a Grammar School boy himself and carried a heart that Still retained its youth. Nothing, .therefgre, more 'natural than that he should become attached to the boys , of the school. The boys loved him, and when he paid visits to them in school, or addressed them at the gatherings when sessions closed, he never failed to impress, upon them his., own motto, " Whatsoever thy, hand findeth to dot do it with thy -might" ; nor did he forget. -to write them a scrap of poetry or genial quip for their breaking-up day, and when he -went to live in the country at 'Kersall Cell he made his visits as usual and caryied in his pocket the usual reCitation Or set of verses.

at the church which is now the Cathedral Church of Manchester, and naturally some copies of the lines would go to friends and fellow-singers there. One of them, • '-by some happy circumstance, -fell into the hands of John Wainwright, the organi_st incJ choir- master.

div.head: WHY NOT ONE .FOR DOLLY?
div.p: WHY NOT ONE .FOR DOLLY?

It was while .the kindly doctor was at work upon one of these poems that an incident occurred which has left us all very grateful. Dorothy Byrom, his daughter, entered the little gthdy• and intemunted'-ivith the words,—"l I,vish to ask a favour, Father." This was very unusual,' and drew the remark, " Well, Dolly, that is curious. But what is it?"

• " Well, it is this: You are writing poetry for. boys of the school who up NOT live, at your house, and I want you to write some for the girl who DOES," - There was only one answer to this, and the doctor laughed heartily, as he took up his quill again. •

Dolly had.scored ; how admirably riot. even She nor .the doctor could have foreseen. By that stroke of girlish.ingenuity she had done some- thing that was to make both of them famous for ever. " What will suit Dolly?" the, fond father was asking in his calmer moments. Then came the idea " Why not some Christmas lines that. she could copy on .Christmas cards and send to her friends?"
The idea pleased him and he applied himself to the task. • •

Whether the lines flowed easily, or whether by slow effort, we do not know, but a few days afterwards, when Dolly came- to _breakfast, piece of paper peeped out from under her plate. It bore the title "Christmas Day for Doily,- and she began to read: Christians, awake, salute the happy morn,
Whereon the Saviour of the world was born. There were forty-eight lines in all. Dolly read them through, an then looked across thc table to say, "Thank you, father; it is beau- tiful."
Dolly had a -task for that winter morning. Copy after copy was written., and the .sheets went out as greetings to her dearest friends. • It ought to be said that she was a chorister

div.head: JOHN WAINWRIGHT.
div.p: JOHN WAINWRIGHT.

Wainwright, who had belonged to Si7Ockport, and who had been a chorister of St. Alary's Church in that town, was a capital musician. The lines arrested him, and he saw in them the 61.1bSitill(-26 01 a fino Ultls hymn, No such idea had been t4l ae halt. of br. Tiyrom. lie had written the forty-eight lines in con- tinuous fashion, without thought of stanza, and indeed without any idea that they would ever ;r2.l*Pl beyond the circle of. Miss Dolly's friends. But John Wainwright Saw that they could easily easily be shaped into a hymn,

These are the lines as he found them : Christians, awake, salute the happy mcrn. Whereon the Saviour of the world was born; Rise, to adore the mystery of love, Which hosts of angels chanted from above; With them the joyful tidings first begun Of God Incarnate, and the Virgin's Son Then to the watchful shepherds it was toTd, Who heard the angelic herald's voice— " Behold ! " I bring good tidings of a Saviour's birth "To you and all the nations upon earth; "This day hath God fulfilled his promis'd word; "This day is born a Saviour, Christ the Lord: "In David's city, shepherds, ye shall find "The long-foretold Redeemer of Mankind. " Wrapt up in swaddling clothes, the Babe Divine "Lies in a manger; this shall be your sign." He spake, and straightway the celestial choir, In hymns of joy, unknown before, conspire;

The praises of redeeming love they sing, And Heaven's whole orb with Hallelujahs ring. "God's highest glory" was their anthem still; " Peace upon earth, and mutual good will." To Bethlehem straight th' enlightened shep- herds ran, To see the wonder God had wrought for man, And found with Joseph and the blessed Maid, Her Son, the Saviour, in a manger laid. Amaz'd, the wondrous story they proclaim; The first Apostles of his infant fame; While Mary keeps, and ponders in her heart, The heav'nly vision, which the swains impart. They to their flocks, still praising God, return, And their glad hearts within their bosoms burn. Let us, like these good shepherds, then, employ Our grateful voices to proclaim the lay; Like Mary, let us ponder in our mind God's wondrous love in saving lost mankind: Artless, and watchful, as those favour'd swains, While virgin meekness in the heart remains, trace we the Babe, who has retriev'd our loss, From his poor manger to His bitter cross;

Treading his steps, assisted by His grace, man's first Heavenly state again takes. place. . Then may we hope Angelic thrones among, To sing, redeem'd, a glad triumphal song; He that was born upon this joyful day, Around us all, his glory shall display; Sav'd by His love, incessant we shall sing Of angels, and of angel-Men the King. A glnnce al, a hynnt-book vill reveal:- his SkilfulLgroupilig of the lines. :His tune W(IS firSt jotted in rough fashion in his notebook, and was'intmed "Stoek-porl," in honour of .his native town.

-The next practice night ,at the Cathedral brought a pleasalit surprise to the choristers and a delightful little secret. They were to learn the tune and memorise the hymn, and then, with the first stroke of Christmas morn- ing, , waken- the doctor and his daughter by singing " Christians, awake," under his windOW. SO the .tune pealed out from the organ, anti the noble hymn echoed from the arches.

• Between the hour of eleven and twelve on Christmas Eve the singers tramped out ,to Kersall Cell. They Crept quietly through the garden gate and waited for :the important Moment., The -distant church bell: sounded twelve, and "Christians, awake," rang, out on • the night air. The effeit upon the doctor and his beloved Dorothy was one of joyful excitement. " Dolly Dolly Are you. awake?" 'came a voice from the doctor's room." -•

Of course, Dolly Was awake; and her face at the Window. It was a fair night, very cold, and icicles glistened in the Inoonlight. " Oh, father," came a rapturous cry, " Isn't it- really grand?" "It is indeed, Dolly. I thought it must be the angels' song for Christmas Morn." - Dolly, with her face close to the leaded panes, grasped the circumstance. There was John Wainwright swinging his hand to give the time, and the singers were her own friends. The words were those upon her Christmas card, and the tune wak one, of their own making. It was- too cold for the doctor to rise, or he would have walked to the window to give his blessing. Dolly opened the casement and showed her lace. "Good morning. and God bless you," cried voices from below, and the singers filed back through the garden gate. .." Christians, awake," .had been sung for the Frrst time under the twinWg stars, and its writer lay with tears of gladness in his eyes. It was the Christmas Morning of .1749. Dr. Byrom passed Wily, honoured and beloved, at the end of 1763—a hundred and fifty years ago. A. M.

div.head: OLD WEAVER'S GOLDEN WEDDING.
div.p: OLD WEAVER'S GOLDEN WEDDING.

Mr iand Mrs. W. Gardiner, of Swan-Street, Blackburn, will celebrate their golden wedding on Christmas Eve. Though 73 years of age, Mr. Gardiner is still a weaver at Messrs. Codding- ton's Wellington mill, and he rises each morning at four o'clock and is at the -mill -before 5.30 to Prepare for the other operatives. Mr. Gardiner has been a trade unionist for 57 years without a break.

div.head: WORLD OF LETTERS
div.p: WORLD OF LETTERS
New Boukb.
Songs from Books. By lludyard Kipling London: Macmillan and Co., Ltd.

As readers of Mr. Kipling are aware, many: Of his books have verses interspersed between the different stories. These he has colleeted arcd 'published in the volume under -review. It is well that this has been done, for though it is pot a complete collection of his poems, it brings into prominenCe verses of striking force and beauty, which might have been passed with little notice when they were only published as chapter headings. A little' While ago when the appointment of a Poet Laureate was in question, there was a general opinion, as shown by the letters appear- ing in the newspapers, that the office should be conferred upon Mr. Kipling. The powers that be thought otherwisc.t. \\Ye, .need AO. discuss N,vl letthey auela e wisely or un-N-N.:ISt'AY., tu-1- at _ any rate it is not difficult to understand 'why the public voice was raised in favour of Mr. Kipling. It is true, he is not the author of-any great epic poem. He .is possibly much better. known by his stories than his verses, though it is probable that some of these 'latter will live ‘liert the former are forgotten. This is a demo- ,.!ratic age, and he has caught its spirit.. In spite of all that is said about the mad race for wealth and pleasure, there is a nobler, more ,Imperial spirit in our English people to-day-77a desire for the growth and Strengthening Of ottr Empire, and a confidence that this Will be for the. ad- vantage of • the whole world. We believe this 'ling spreads deeply and.widely, .and because in his verses Mr. Kipling gives expression to it be may be taken as the true representative of he Britisfi people. He has travelled much, and seen the outposts of our Empire, and his 'verses ring with pride in our past, and hope for the future, if we are faithful to our trust. • The songs front books are of a varied char- acter. Some are of the East, some of the West, sonic of the past, some of the present., but in all of them there is much of wisdom and much of beauty. "The heritage" and the " Children's Song are worthy to rank with " Recessional."
The Seven Cries from the Cross. By the Hey E. Morgan, Padgate.

The very appearance of the Bev. E. Morgan's booklet, "The Seven Cries froni the Cross;" tempts one to purchase, and we are quite sure, from an inspection of its contents, that none need hesitate about succumbing to the tempta- tion. The devotional tone of the book, well maintained throughout, is certainty healthy, and we note here and there a freshness of treatment that is most welcome. If we were to find fault with the, book at all we should- say that its author had, Condensed his matter unduly, for there is sufficient in these few pages for a much larger volume. We will not complain, however, even about that, for it means we -get plenty for our money. The Bev. W. A. Beckett, or \V. 11. Smith and Sons, will supply.

div.head: Literary Gleanings.
div.p: Literary Gleanings.
WEIRD STORY.

One of the most devoted bookmen of our day is Sir William Robertson Nicoll, and he has just published a volume of " Bookman's Letters." We cull the following creepy story Iroin the chapter •4' Stranger than Fiction'":— The husband of a ct rtain lady was a singular chara(ter, and passionately devoted to, anti- quarian pursuits. He converted the upper part of his house into a-museum, and built a special room for himself, lighted and ventilated in a peculiar manner. Among his other peculiar- .ities there were two skeletons, which he dusted and brushed himself. The dread of the skele- tons was so great that not one of the servants willingly approached the staircase leading to the room in which they were deposited. They all united in declaring that very strange sounds were licard to proceed iron') the floor. By and by his wife died, and he came into possession of an ample fortunet-- A great change passed over .his appearance. He began to be spruce in his dress, gay and courteous ih his mannerS,. and accessible to strangers. By and by he prevailed on a very beautiful young lady, a portionless daughter of a curate, to become his Wife. He told her plainly beforehand that if she married him she must submit to Some. dis- agreeable restrictions, as he had made up,his mind never to leave .the town in which be resided; there would therefore be no bridal tour. The lady agreed, and she WAS treated with .a great deal of kindness, and allowed .iceasionally to leave the' home, though her imsband never accompanied her in any of her ,xcursions. In about ten years'after the mar- the vault in which .the remains of the first wife were deposited was opened in consequence of some necessary repairs. It appeared, that the undertaker had abstracted the leaden coffin in which the .body had been encased, and' the Nvoodez, one fell to pieces, disclosing the corpse. The perfect state of the body attracted atten- tion, a face,' ghastly it is true, but still un- flecayed, appeared beneath the 'mouldering shroud. On examination the supposed corpse- Droved to be a wax figure, and ,amoutcry arose that' murder had been committed. One of the magistrates of the plare proceeded to the anti- quarian's abode, and bluntly told him the facts. After a few mil-Rites 'of strong perturbation the man exclaimed: Gentlemen', I have a living witness to prove my innocence of the crime imputed 'to me." lie led the way to the upper floor, opened several doors, and .brought out a person who was no other than his first wife. Tie had contrived to keep her in close c.onflne7 intent during this long portion. of her existence. The agitation produced ~by the discovery and the dread of consequences brought on an attack. which in a few hours carried off her husband. The second wife quietly removed to the Com- tinent with her children, while the first wife. accustomed to confinement, seemed to have lost all enterprise and energy, and was quite, content to occupy the part of the house in which she had endured so tedious an imprisonment.

My dear Children,—

To judge who were worthy pf prizes was a tusk beyond my power. I read and re-read all the letters received—they numbered 68—and could. not make up my mind. I button-holed nearly everybody in the office to get their opinion,, and after.o bit they grew tired of me, and said I Was an old nuisance. Still I pey- sisted in asking them to help me to select the best letters, until finally, when they saw me come, in at one door with a letter in, my hand ! they ran out of the other door. Just when thought I should never be able to decide, it ! occurred to me to send the letters to Santa Claus. I did, and this is his report.
Santa Claus't Selection. Doar .lApte

I am very grateful to all who have sent in letters, and although they have not been suc- cessful now, I hope they will do better in our future competitions. Tlire were some amusing requests. div.head: IHE IRISH QUESTION.
div.p: IHE IRISH QUESTION.
United Irishmen United in Favour
of Mr. Crosfield.
LABOUR CANDIDATE QUESTION.

There was a large attendance in the United Irish League Rooms on Sunday afternoon, when Mr. P. Kelly gave an instructive address on "From Gratton to Redmond."_ Mr. Currie pre- sided, and dealt with what he termed "a lying statement made last week by the Member, who misrepresents Warrington." He said there were only 16 Protestant county councillors in Ireland and that all the rest were Catholics. That was put out as a strong point against the Catholics in Ireland, but on the other hand it was a statement in favour of Home Rule. The councillors were returned by ballot, and if Mr. Smith's statement was true, there was an over- whelming majority in favour of Home Rule. Mter showing that the majority of the best posi- tions in Ireland were given to Protestants, he said it showed where the intolerance came in. Where positions were gifts of Protestant Coun- cils, the Catholics were excluded. There had been no intolerance on the part of the Catholics in Ireland.. (Hear, hear.) CARSON, SMITH AND CO.

Mr. KELLY kept the audience brimful of in- terest from the commencement .to the, conclu- sion, and mingled typical Irish humour with the body of the address. He gave lucid details of the persecutions and sufferings of the people, and said they wanted a Parliament of their own to conduct their own affairs. They should take no notice of Carson, Smith. and Co., but vote for the Liberals, whom he believed would do their best for them. There was nothing but an earthquake to stop Home Rule, and neither Carson and Co. or their wooden guns were going to stop it. (Hear, ihenr, and .applause.) -

div.head: TRAITOR TO HIS COUNTRY.
div.p: A TRAITOR TO HIS COUNTRY.

MT. HANDLEY proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Kelly. Ife had heard that a Labour candidate was going to be put up in Warrington at the next election, lie hoped they would not be so blind as to put: a Labour candidate against such a staunch Home Ruler as Mr. Crosfield. (Ap- , plause.) Any man who voted for a Labour candidate against Home Rule was a traitor to his country. If a Labour man put up the Irish-men were organised better to-day than they had been for 40 years, and the party that went against them would meet a stalwart foe, and he would be one of the first to go against them if they went against Home Rule. (Applause.) • Mr. MAHONEY seconded, and Mr. Horan suP- ported, and said their cause was not for revenge for the past, but justice for the future. (Hear, hear.) , MY. KELLY proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was heartily carried. The CHAIRMAN suitably replied.

div.head: CROSFIELD'S FINE VICTORY.
div.p: CROSFIELD'S FINE VICTORY.

Crosfield's secured a fine victory over Sale Moor at Sankey. The game opened evenly, nice Passing movements emanating from both sides, and it *as some time before the home team opened the score with a good shot from Hodson. This reverse acted as a tonic to the visitors, who now pressed vigorously, and it was only by the good play of the full-backs that the goal was kept safe. Profiting by the fumbling of the. visitors' goalkeeper, Lythgoe rushed a second goal through. Dickson secured the balit from a corner hit, and although hampered by several opponents, from the edge of the circle shot a splendid goal. Half-time arrived with Cros- field's leading three goals to nil. The second half was, to a great extent, similar to the first. The first incident of note was a good individual effort by Bloomer, which ended in that player scoring- his usual goal. Still keeping up the pressure,. Crosfield's added to their scon, Lythgoe scoring with a fast shot. Result: Crosfield's, five goals; Sale Moor, nil.
